name: Predictive Model
diff_siblings: ML learns statistical patterns without explicit rules; Deep Learning uses deep neural networks for automatic hierarchical representations; Classical Statistics derives analytical relationships focusing on inference, interpretability, and theoretical guarantees
strengths: Covers any prediction problem with historical data
Scalable from simple to extremely complex
Controllable trade-off between performance and interpretability
weaknesses: No approach dominates in all problems
recommended_for: Any domain with historical data and identifiable pattern
not_recommended_for: Problems with deterministic rules known a priori
Complete absence of historical data
curiosity: The 'No Free Lunch' theorem (Wolpert, 1996) mathematically proves that no algorithm is universally superior — the best model always depends on the specific problem.

children.name: 1. Machine Learning
children.diff_siblings: ML uses algorithms that learn patterns from data; Deep Learning is a subset with a qualitatively different scale; Classical Statistics prioritizes causal inference and interpretability over predictive performance
strengths: Wide range of algorithms for tabular data
More interpretable than Deep Learning in most cases
weaknesses: Inferior performance to Deep Learning in images, text, and audio
Requires manual feature engineering in many cases
Limited scale compared to large neural networks
recommended_for: Problems with moderate data and need for interpretability
not_recommended_for: Images, audio, and text without specialized feature engineering
Problems that require content generation
children.curiosity: The term 'machine learning' was coined by Arthur Samuel in 1959 while programming an IBM 701 to play checkers — the program improved until it beat its own creator.

children.name: 1.1 Supervised
children.diff_siblings: Supervised uses labeled input-output pairs; Unsupervised discovers structure without labels; Semi-supervised combines both; Reinforcement learns by interacting with the environment via rewards
strengths: High performance when labeled data is abundant
weaknesses: Does not generalize well outside the training distribution
Label bias propagates to the model
recommended_for: Any problem with available ground truth
not_recommended_for: Abundant unlabeled data
When labeling is unfeasible
children.curiosity: The supervised paradigm dominates industrial applications — it is estimated that 80% of models in production use some form of supervision.

children.name: 1.1.1 Regression
children.diff_siblings: Regression predicts continuous values; Classification predicts categories; Time Series predicts ordered sequences; Survival models time until event
strengths: Interpretable output as a numerical value
Intuitive metrics like RMSE and MAE
weaknesses: May require transformations for skewed distributions
not_recommended_for: Categorical outputs
When the response variable is discrete by nature
children.curiosity: Gauss and Legendre developed least squares in the early 19th century to calculate asteroid orbits — regression precedes the modern concept of ML by 150 years.

children.name: GLM (Generalized Linear Models)
children.diff_siblings: GLM generalizes linear regression via a link function and exponential family; GAM adds non-linearity via splines; Mixed Effects add hierarchical group structure
weaknesses: Does not capture complex interactions automatically
recommended_for: When interpretation of coefficients is necessary
not_recommended_for: Highly non-linear relationships without known structure
children.curiosity: Nelder and Wedderburn unified linear, logistic, and Poisson regression under the GLM framework in 1972 — previously, each model was treated as a separate algorithm.

children.name: Gaussian GLM (identity)
children.diff_siblings: Uses Normal distribution with identity link — equivalent to linear regression; the only GLM where the link function is directly linear
strengths: Closed-form analytical solution via least squares
Maximum statistical efficiency with Normal residuals
recommended_for: Continuous variables with approximately Normal errors
not_recommended_for: Count data, proportions, or time-to-event
children.curiosity: Least squares estimation was published by Legendre in 1805 and Gauss in 1809 — one of the first priority disputes in the history of applied mathematics.

children.name: Binomial / Logistic GLM
children.diff_siblings: Logit link transforms probability into log-odds — for binary response; differs from Gaussian by modeling probabilities and from Poisson by having a fixed denominator
weaknesses: Assumes linearity in the log-odds space
Inferior performance to Gradient Boosting on complex data
not_recommended_for: More than two classes without multinomial adaptation
Highly non-linear relationships
children.curiosity: Logistic regression was developed by David Cox in 1958. Despite being over 60 years old, it remains the most used model in bank credit approval due to regulatory requirements for interpretability.

children.name: Poisson GLM
children.diff_siblings: Log link for non-negative count data; assumes mean = variance — which rarely happens in real data; basis for more sophisticated count models
strengths: Natural for modeling rates and counts
recommended_for: Count of rare events: accidents, crimes, hospitalizations
not_recommended_for: Data with overdispersion — Negative Binomial
When zeros are very frequent — ZIP
children.curiosity: Siméon-Denis Poisson developed the distribution in 1838 studying errors in judicial judgments. Widespread statistical application came 100 years later with Bortkiewicz in 1898.

children.name: Gamma GLM
children.diff_siblings: For positive continuous variables with variance proportional to the square of the mean — differs from Gaussian by being asymmetric and from Tweedie by being purely continuous
strengths: Suitable for positive and asymmetric data
not_recommended_for: Data with frequent zeros — Tweedie
Approximately symmetric distribution — Gaussian
children.curiosity: The Gamma distribution was formalized by Karl Pearson in the early 20th century. It is the standard distribution in actuarial science for modeling claim severity.

children.name: Inverse Gaussian GLM
children.diff_siblings: For positive data with tails even heavier than Gamma — variance proportional to the cube of the mean; niche between Gamma and extremely heavy-tailed distributions
strengths: Models phenomena with very high variance
Suitable for first-passage times in diffusion processes
recommended_for: Financial data with extremely heavy tails
not_recommended_for: Most practical problems — Gamma is already sufficient
children.curiosity: The Inverse Gaussian distribution was named by Wald in 1947 for being the 'inverse' distribution of the Gaussian in the sense of the Wiener process.

children.name: GLM Tweedie
children.diff_siblings: Parametric family that unifies Gaussian (p=0), Poisson (p=1), Gamma (p=2) via parameter p — the only GLM that naturally models a mixture of zeros and positive continuous values
strengths: Unifies multiple distributions in a single parameter p
Models distributions with mass at zero and a continuous tail
recommended_for: Insurance premiums: mixture of zeros and positive values
not_recommended_for: Purely continuous data — Gamma is simpler
When p can be determined by context
children.curiosity: Maurice Tweedie described the family in 1984. With p≈1.5, it is the 'Poisson-Gamma compound distribution' — standard in the insurance industry for aggregate claims.

children.name: GLM Quasi-likelihood
children.diff_siblings: Relaxes the full distribution assumption — specifies only the relationship between mean and variance; useful when data exhibit overdispersion but the exact distribution is unknown
strengths: Does not require a full distribution
Useful for overdispersion in count data
not_recommended_for: When AIC/BIC are necessary
Severe overdispersion — Negative Binomial
children.curiosity: Wedderburn introduced quasi-likelihood in 1974. The approach anticipated modern concepts of robust estimation and GEE (Generalized Estimating Equations).

children.name: Ordinal Regression (Proportional Odds)
children.diff_siblings: For ordinal response variables (e.g., 1-5 stars) — models cumulative probabilities; differs from Logistic by preserving order without assuming equal distances
strengths: Preserves the natural order of categories
weaknesses: Assumes proportional odds (testable but frequently violated)
recommended_for: Likert scales, satisfaction levels, disease grades
not_recommended_for: Categories without natural order — multinomial logistic
children.curiosity: Proposed by Peter McCullagh in 1980. It is the standard model in clinical pharmacology for analyzing pain scales and drug efficacy.

children.name: Multinomial Regression
children.diff_siblings: Extension of logistic for K>2 unordered classes — uses K-1 logistic equations with a reference category; differs from Ordinal by not assuming order among categories
strengths: Interpretation via log-odds relative to the base category
recommended_for: Choice of transport mode, product type
not_recommended_for: Classes with natural order — Ordinal
Many rare classes
children.curiosity: The IIA property of multinomial regression was described by the 'Blue/Red Bus Paradox': adding a blue bus identical to the red one incorrectly splits the market equally with all.

children.name: GAM (Generalized Additive Models)
children.diff_siblings: GAM extends GLM by replacing linear terms with smooth non-parametric functions; MARS uses piecewise linear functions; Mixed Effects add group structure to GLM
strengths: Captures non-linearity without specifying functional form
Visual interpretation via partial dependence plots
weaknesses: Does not natively capture interactions between predictors
Risk of overfitting with many spline knots
recommended_for: Non-linear relationships with need for interpretability
not_recommended_for: Complex interactions between many variables
When performance surpasses interpretability
children.curiosity: Hastie and Tibshirani proposed GAMs in 1986. In 2021, Google published Neural Additive Models — showing that the central idea remains relevant decades later.

children.name: Classic GAM (smoothing splines)
children.diff_siblings: Uses cubic splines for each predictor — differs from GAMLSS by modeling only the mean and from GAMM by having no random effects
strengths: Intuitive visualization of the effect of each variable
Degree of smoothing selectable via cross-validation
The mgcv library in R is a benchmark for maturity
recommended_for: Variables with curvilinear effects in epidemiology and ecology
not_recommended_for: Many variables with interactions — XGBoost performs better
children.curiosity: Simon Wood developed the mgcv package in R, now cited in tens of thousands of papers. The automatic selection of the smoothing parameter via GCV was a fundamental practical advance.

children.name: GAMLSS (Location, Scale, Shape)
children.diff_siblings: Extends GAM by modeling not only the mean but also variance and shape — the only one that models the full distribution as a function of predictors
weaknesses: Many more parameters than classic GAM
not_recommended_for: Simple problems where classic GAM is sufficient
children.curiosity: WHO child growth curves are estimated using GAMLSS — every child on the planet is compared to models trained with this method.

children.name: GAMM (GAM with mixed effects)
children.diff_siblings: Combines GAM's non-parametric smoothers with random effects — captures non-linearity and intra-group correlation
strengths: Combines advantages of GAM and LMM
not_recommended_for: Independent data — classic GAM is sufficient
children.curiosity: GAMM unifies two frameworks developed independently in the 1980s-90s. Integration only became feasible with the PQL algorithm and modern processors.

children.name: Linear
children.diff_siblings: Linear models assume a direct relationship between predictors and response; GLMs use link function for non-Gaussian; non-linear models capture curvatures
recommended_for: Approximately linear relationships with a need for interpretation
not_recommended_for: Non-linear relationships without adequate transformation
children.curiosity: Linear regression by least squares has an analytical solution: β = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy. For matrices with more than 10,000 columns, this inversion starts to become challenging.

children.name: Simple Linear Regression
children.diff_siblings: A single continuous predictor — simplest case; lower risk of multicollinearity; direct geometric interpretation as a line in the plane
strengths: Immediate interpretation: β₁ units of Y per unit of X
weaknesses: Rarely adequate for real-world problems with multiple predictors
recommended_for: Exploratory analysis of the relationship between two variables
not_recommended_for: Problems with multiple predictors
children.curiosity: Gauss used this principle to predict the position of the asteroid Ceres in 1801 — the first documented application of regression for prediction.

children.name: Multiple Linear Regression
children.diff_siblings: Multiple predictors — distinguishes itself from simple regression by potential multicollinearity and ceteris paribus interpretation; without regularization
recommended_for: Causal inference with control of confounding variables
not_recommended_for: High dimensionality (p > n) — use regularization
children.curiosity: Francis Galton invented the concept of 'regression to the mean' in 1885 studying heights of parents and children — the name 'regression' comes from this study.

children.name: Ridge (L2)
children.diff_siblings: L2 penalty shrinks coefficients towards zero without zeroing them — more stable with correlated predictors than Lasso
strengths: Closed-form analytical solution even with regularization
not_recommended_for: When sparsity is desired — Lasso
children.curiosity: Hoerl and Kennard proposed Ridge in 1970. The name 'ridge' comes from the geometry of the regularized loss surface.

children.name: Lasso (L1)
children.diff_siblings: L1 penalty produces sparse solutions with coefficients exactly zero — performs variable selection; unstable with highly correlated predictors
weaknesses: Does not have a closed-form analytical solution
recommended_for: High dimensionality with suspicion of true sparsity
not_recommended_for: Highly correlated predictors — ElasticNet
children.curiosity: Robert Tibshirani proposed Lasso in 1996. Sparsity came as a surprise — he did not anticipate that L1 penalty would produce exact zeros.

children.name: ElasticNet
children.diff_siblings: Combines L1 and L2 — stable with correlated predictors and still performs selection; parameter α controls the mix between L1 and L2
strengths: Selects groups of correlated variables together
weaknesses: Slower than Lasso or Ridge alone
recommended_for: Data with groups of correlated variables
not_recommended_for: Maximum sparsity — Lasso is more aggressive
children.curiosity: Zou and Hastie proposed ElasticNet in 2005 motivated by genomics problems where genes in pathways tend to be correlated.

children.name: PCR (Principal Component Regression)
children.diff_siblings: Reduces dimensionality via PCA before regression — differs from Ridge by transforming the space; from PLS by not using the response variable in component construction
weaknesses: PCA ignores response — components may be irrelevant
not_recommended_for: When interpretability of original coefficients is necessary
children.curiosity: PCR was proposed by Massy in 1965. Components that explain more variance in X may be the least useful for predicting Y — a limitation that motivated PLS.

children.name: PLS (Partial Least Squares)
children.diff_siblings: Builds latent components that maximize covariance with the response — uses Y in the construction; differs from PCR by incorporating response information
weaknesses: Assumes linear relationship between components and Y
not_recommended_for: Data with n >> p where OLS already works
children.curiosity: Herman Wold developed PLS in the 1960s. His son Svante Wold popularized it in chemometrics — today it is the standard for NIR spectroscopy calibration in the food industry.

children.name: Stepwise Regression
children.diff_siblings: Sequential variable selection via statistical criterion (AIC, p-value) — discrete (variable enters or leaves); unstable — small changes in data generate different models
weaknesses: Unstable: small changes change the model
Does not control false positive rate with many predictors
not_recommended_for: High dimensionality — Lasso or ElasticNet
When reproducibility is critical
children.curiosity: Frank Harrell extensively documented the problems of Stepwise. It is estimated to appear in 30-40% of clinical articles with multiple regression — a concerning persistence given its known problems.

children.name: Best Subset Selection
children.diff_siblings: Evaluates all 2ᵖ subsets of predictors — exhaustive (optimal for the criterion); impractical above ~30 predictors
strengths: Guarantees the best subset for the chosen criterion
weaknesses: Computational cost O(2ᵖ) — unfeasible with p > 30
recommended_for: Small problems where guaranteed optimality is necessary
not_recommended_for: p > 30 — use Lasso
When computation time is relevant
children.curiosity: In 2020, Bertsimas et al. published an algorithm for Best Subset up to p=1000 using mixed-integer programming — resurrecting the method with modern hardware.

children.name: Non-Linear
children.diff_siblings: Capture curvatures; GLMs use specific link function; Mixed Effects add hierarchical structure; Kernel projects into high-dimensional space
strengths: Capture patterns that linear models cannot
recommended_for: Curvilinear relationships between predictors and response
not_recommended_for: When linearity is reasonable — simpler models
children.curiosity: The Universal Approximation Theorem (Cybenko, 1989) showed that any continuous function can be approximated by a neural network — but did not specify the required size.

children.name: Polynomial Regression
children.diff_siblings: Extension of linear with degree d terms — global model (less stable than splines); no adaptive knots like MARS
strengths: Can approximate any continuous function with sufficient degree
weaknesses: High-degree polynomials oscillate at the edges (Runge effect)
recommended_for: Simple curvilinear relationships with limited range
not_recommended_for: High degree (>4)
Extrapolation beyond the data
children.curiosity: The 'Runge phenomenon' (1901) showed that increasing the degree can worsen the approximation — motivating the development of splines.

children.name: Quantile Regression
children.diff_siblings: Estimates conditional quantiles (median, P90, P10) instead of the mean — without assumptions about error distribution; robust to outliers
strengths: Robust to outliers in the response
recommended_for: When distribution tails are of interest (Value at Risk)
Asymmetric data or data with outliers
not_recommended_for: When interest is only in the conditional mean
children.curiosity: Roger Koenker received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2021 — in part for this work — 43 years after the original publication.

children.name: Isotonic Regression
children.diff_siblings: Estimates a non-decreasing (or non-increasing) function — without specifying form beyond monotonicity; solution via pool adjacent violators
weaknesses: Solution is a step function — not smooth
recommended_for: When monotonicity is guaranteed by the domain
not_recommended_for: Multiple predictors
When relationship is not monotonic
children.curiosity: The 'Pool Adjacent Violators' algorithm solves Isotonic Regression in O(n) and is still the standard — its mathematical elegance is remarkable.

children.name: Tobit Regression
children.diff_siblings: For response variables censored at a limit (e.g., non-negative expenses) — explicitly models censoring; differs from Survival by assuming Normality
strengths: Models censoring in a statistically correct way
Unbiased estimates when censoring is informative
weaknesses: Sensitive to deviations from Normality in the censored tail
recommended_for: Censored data: expenses, working hours, consumption with lower limit
not_recommended_for: Interval or random censoring — Cox PH is more suitable
children.curiosity: James Tobin proposed the model in 1958. The model was named in his honor by Arthur Goldberger — not for the Nobel that Tobin won in 1981.

children.name: Beta Regression
children.diff_siblings: For responses in the interval (0,1) such as proportions — differs from Logistic by modeling continuous values, not probabilities of binary events
strengths: Models skewness and bimodality in proportions
weaknesses: Does not handle exact zeros and ones
Requires specification of the precision equation
not_recommended_for: Binary variables — Logistic
Data with frequent zeros and ones
children.curiosity: Ferrari and Cribari-Neto formalized Beta Regression in 2004. The Beta distribution was described by Euler in the 18th century — application in regression waited 250 years.

children.name: MARS (Multivariate Adaptive Regression Splines)
children.diff_siblings: Piecewise linear functions with adaptive knots — discovers knots automatically; more interpretable than neural networks; different from Splines due to automatic knots
recommended_for: Non-linear relationships with need for interpretability
not_recommended_for: Very large datasets — Boosting is more efficient
children.curiosity: Jerome Friedman proposed MARS in 1991 — the same author of Gradient Boosting. MARS anticipated many ideas of modern models.

children.name: Spline Regression
children.diff_siblings: Piecewise polynomial functions with continuity at knots — without oscillation of the global polynomial (no Runge's phenomenon); knots can be specified by domain
weaknesses: Knots need to be specified a priori
recommended_for: Instrument calibration with known physical knots
not_recommended_for: When knot position is unknown — GAM
children.curiosity: Splines came from flexible metal rulers used by naval draftsmen in the 1940s. The statistical version was formalized by Grace Wahba in the 1970s.

children.name: SUR (Seemingly Unrelated Regression)
children.diff_siblings: System of regression equations with correlated errors — gains efficiency via residual correlation; differs from VAR by not modeling temporal causality
strengths: More efficient estimation than separate regressions
weaknesses: Zero gain when errors are independent
not_recommended_for: Independent errors — separate OLS is equivalent
Causality between equations — VAR
children.curiosity: Arnold Zellner proposed SUR in 1962. The central result: GLS on the system is more efficient than equation-by-equation OLS when errors are correlated.

children.name: M5 Model Tree
children.diff_siblings: Decision tree with linear models at the leaves — more accurate than CART for regression; differs from CART by having models, not constants, at the leaves
strengths: More accurate than CART for regression
Interpretable: shows regime and linear equation
recommended_for: Data with distinct regimes where each regime has linear behavior
not_recommended_for: Purely non-linear relationships
When GBM is feasible — tends to outperform M5
children.curiosity: J. Ross Quinlan proposed M5 in 1992. The model anticipated the 'mixture of experts' idea that would inspire modern Deep Learning architectures.

children.name: Mixed Effects
children.diff_siblings: Incorporate hierarchical group structure via random effects; GLMs model non-Gaussian distribution without groups; Kernel captures non-linearity via projection
strengths: More efficient than OLS with hierarchical data
weaknesses: More complex to fit and diagnose
recommended_for: Longitudinal data, repeated measures, panel data
not_recommended_for: Data without hierarchical structure
When groups have many observations
children.curiosity: Ronald Fisher introduced variance components in 1918 studying genetic inheritance. The term 'mixed effects' was consolidated by Henderson in 1950 in animal breeding.

children.name: LMM / lmer (Linear Mixed Models)
children.diff_siblings: Continuous response variable with random effects — differs from GLMM by assuming Normality; from nlme by assuming linearity
strengths: REML estimation provides unbiased variance estimates
weaknesses: Convergence may fail with complex structures
not_recommended_for: Binary or count responses — GLMM
children.curiosity: Douglas Bates developed lme4 in R, now cited in tens of thousands of scientific papers.

children.name: GLMM (Generalized Linear Mixed Models)
children.diff_siblings: Combines non-Gaussian distributions from GLM with random effects from LMM — for hierarchical binary/count responses
weaknesses: Likelihood integral has no closed form
recommended_for: Binary or count data with clustering
not_recommended_for: Normal continuous response — LMM is simpler
children.curiosity: GLMM estimation requires numerical integration via Laplace approximation — adapted from quantum physics: uses the curvature of the function at its maximum to estimate the integral.

children.name: nlme (Nonlinear Mixed Effects)
children.diff_siblings: Random effects in nonlinear models like pharmacokinetic compartments — parameters have direct physical interpretation (half-life, Cmax)
strengths: Models individual trajectories with known shape
not_recommended_for: When functional form is not known — GAM
children.curiosity: The nlme package was developed by Pinheiro and Bates. The FDA uses NLME as the standard for pharmacokinetic analysis in new drug submissions.

children.name: HLM (Hierarchical Linear Models)
children.diff_siblings: Equivalent to LMM with social science terminology — emphasizes interpretation of coefficients at each hierarchical level
strengths: Decomposes variance between and within groups
weaknesses: HLM software has a paid license
recommended_for: Educational research: students in classes in schools
not_recommended_for: When lme4 flexibility is needed
children.curiosity: Raudenbush and Bryk popularized HLM in 1992. The model was motivated by the study of 'school effect' — separating how much of the variation in grades is from the school vs. the student.

children.name: BART (Bayesian Additive Regression Trees)
children.diff_siblings: Bayesian ensemble of trees with priors over structure — provides credibility intervals; differs from RF by Bayesian inference instead of optimization
recommended_for: When prediction uncertainty is as important as the point estimate
not_recommended_for: When training speed is a priority
Datasets with more than 100k rows
children.curiosity: Chipman, George, and McCulloch proposed BART in 2010. Jennifer Hill adapted it for causal inference in 2011 — today BART is the reference for estimating heterogeneous causal effects.

children.name: Kernel-based
children.diff_siblings: Project data into high-dimensional space via similarity function — capture non-linearity without specifying shape; different from trees for creating smooth boundaries
strengths: Kernel trick avoids explicit computation in high dimension
weaknesses: Scale poorly with n — cost O(n²) to O(n³)
Kernel and regularization require careful tuning
not_recommended_for: Big data — neural networks and boosting scale better
children.curiosity: Vladimir Vapnik and Alexey Chervonenkis developed SVM theory in the 1960s in the USSR. The kernel trick was discovered by Aizermann in 1964.

children.name: SVR (Support Vector Regression)
children.diff_siblings: Regression version of SVM with epsilon tube — predictions inside the tube generate no penalty; sparse solution via support vectors
strengths: Robust to outliers in the response
weaknesses: Three hyperparameters (C, ε, kernel) require CV
recommended_for: Medium-sized data with non-linear relationship and outliers
not_recommended_for: Big data — LightGBM is much faster
When prediction intervals are needed — GPR
children.curiosity: Vapnik et al. proposed SVR in 1997. The epsilon tube creates a zone of indifference that makes the solution sparse — only support vectors outside the tube determine the model.

children.name: Kernel Ridge Regression
children.diff_siblings: Ridge regression in the kernel feature space — closed-form analytical solution; differs from SVR by using quadratic loss; from GPR by being point estimation
strengths: Dual equivalent of Ridge in kernel space
More numerically stable than SVM with noise
not_recommended_for: Large datasets — approximate GPR or GBM
When sparsity is desired
children.curiosity: The equivalence between Kernel Ridge and GPR with a specific covariance kernel unites Bayesian inference and kernel methods — the same model seen from different perspectives.

children.name: Gaussian Process Regression (GPR)
children.diff_siblings: Non-parametric Bayesian regression with posterior distribution over functions — the only one that naturally quantifies uncertainty via posterior
strengths: Any kernel defines a different prior over functions
weaknesses: Choice of kernel greatly affects the result
recommended_for: Bayesian optimization where uncertainty guides exploration
not_recommended_for: Big data — cubic cost is prohibitive
When uncertainty is not needed — KRR or SVR
children.curiosity: Kriging — the geostatistical precursor of GPR — was developed by Danie Krige in 1951 for estimating gold reserves in South Africa.

children.name: Instance-based
children.diff_siblings: Memorize training data and make predictions by similarity — lazy learners; differ from parametric models by not learning a compact representation
recommended_for: Datasets with complex local patterns and fast training required
not_recommended_for: Very large datasets
High dimensionality without feature selection
children.curiosity: KNN was one of the first algorithms in ML, proposed by Fix and Hodges in 1951 in a military technical report.

children.name: KNN Regression
children.diff_siblings: Average of K nearest neighbors — differs from Radius Neighbors by using a fixed number of neighbors; from KNN classification by aggregating continuous values
weaknesses: Slow for inference on large datasets
Noise in data directly affects predictions
not_recommended_for: High dimensionality — 'curse of dimensionality'
Large datasets
children.curiosity: Cover and Hart (1967) showed that the error of 1-NN converges to at most 2× the optimal Bayes error — surprisingly good for such a simple algorithm.

children.name: Radius Neighbors Regression
children.diff_siblings: Average of neighbors within a fixed radius r — variable number of neighbors; can return NaN in sparse regions
strengths: Number of neighbors adapts to local density
weaknesses: Can fail with points having no neighbors within the radius
recommended_for: Geospatial data with defined physical neighborhood
not_recommended_for: Uniform data — KNN is simpler
When prediction guarantee for all points is required
children.curiosity: Radius Neighbors captures a different intuition than KNN: 'natural neighborhood' instead of 'K nearest'. In geospatial data, a 5 km radius is more interpretable than '10 nearest neighbors'.

children.name: 1.1.2 Classification
children.diff_siblings: Predicts discrete categories; Regression predicts continuous values; the distinction is that the output is a label without natural numerical order
strengths: Metrics like accuracy and AUC are intuitive
recommended_for: Medical diagnosis, fraud detection, image classification
not_recommended_for: Continuous responses — regression is more informative
children.curiosity: Bayes' theorem is the foundation of optimal classification: the Bayes classifier minimizes error by classifying each point into the class with the highest posterior probability.

children.name: Probabilistic / Bayesian
children.diff_siblings: Model P(class|features) via Bayes; differ from linear methods that model boundaries directly; provide calibrated probabilities by construction
strengths: Work well with few data using priors
not_recommended_for: Complex non-linear relationships — trees outperform
children.curiosity: Thomas Bayes never published the theorem in his lifetime — it was published posthumously in 1763 by Richard Price.

children.name: Gaussian Naive Bayes
children.diff_siblings: Continuous features with conditional Normal distribution — 'Naive' due to conditional independence; differs from Multinomial by not requiring counts
recommended_for: Classification with continuous features and few data
not_recommended_for: Highly correlated features
children.curiosity: Despite the 'naive' name, it works well because decision boundaries are robust even when independence is violated — what matters is the order of probabilities.

children.name: Multinomial Naive Bayes
children.diff_siblings: For discrete features (word counts) — differs from Gaussian by using Multinomial distribution; from Bernoulli by modeling frequencies, not presence/absence
strengths: Fast and scalable for large vocabularies
weaknesses: Conditional independence is a strong assumption
not_recommended_for: Continuous features — Gaussian
children.curiosity: Multinomial Naive Bayes was the basis for the first effective spam filters in the 2000s. Paul Graham's 'A Plan for Spam' (2002) popularized the approach.

children.name: Naive Bayes Bernoulli
children.diff_siblings: Binary features (presence/absence) — penalizes the absence of words; different from Multinomial which uses counts
strengths: Penalizes absence of features — advantageous in short texts
weaknesses: Inferior performance to Multinomial in long texts
not_recommended_for: Data with relevant frequency information — Multinomial
children.curiosity: In email classification, Bernoulli NB outperforms Multinomial NB in short messages: for 10-word spam, knowing if 'viagra' appears is more useful than how many times.

children.name: Complement Naive Bayes
children.diff_siblings: Estimates parameters using data from complementary classes — corrects the bias of Multinomial in imbalanced data; inverts the probabilistic reasoning
strengths: Better than Multinomial NB in imbalanced data
More stable estimates with rare classes
recommended_for: Text classification with very imbalanced classes
not_recommended_for: Balanced data — Multinomial NB is equivalent
children.curiosity: Rennie et al. proposed CNB in 2003. Instead of modeling 'how typical this class is', it models 'how atypical it is of other classes' — more robust with few examples.

children.name: LDA (Linear Discriminant Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: Finds a linear projection that maximizes separation between classes — differs from QDA by assuming equal covariances; from Logistic by modeling P(X|class) instead of P(class|X)
weaknesses: Number of components limited to K-1
recommended_for: Preprocessing for simultaneous visualization and classification
not_recommended_for: Classes with very different shapes — QDA
Non-normal data
children.curiosity: Ronald Fisher developed LDA in 1936 using 4 features to classify 3 Iris species — the most cited dataset in the history of machine learning.

children.name: QDA (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: Quadratic version of LDA with covariances separated by class — more flexible but with many more parameters: O(p²) per class
strengths: Quadratic boundaries capture different shapes per class
not_recommended_for: Small samples — LDA is more stable
Many features — regularized QDA is necessary
children.curiosity: With p=10 features and K=3 classes, QDA has 30× more parameters than LDA — the classic bias-variance trade-off in its most visible form.

children.name: Bayesian Network
children.diff_siblings: Directed acyclic graph with probabilistic dependencies — differs from Naive Bayes by modeling dependencies between features; from discriminative models by modeling joint distribution
strengths: Incorporates domain knowledge into the structure
recommended_for: Medical diagnosis with known causal structure
not_recommended_for: Many continuous variables without causal structure
Pure predictive performance
children.curiosity: Judea Pearl developed the framework in the 1980s and received the Turing Award in 2011. Pearl argues that Bayesian Networks are the foundation for causal reasoning.

children.name: Linear Models
children.diff_siblings: Construct separation hyperplanes — differ from probabilistic ones by modeling boundaries directly; from trees by creating smooth and global boundaries; from SVMs by not maximizing margin
recommended_for: High dimensionality such as NLP and bioinformatics
not_recommended_for: Non-linear relationships without feature engineering
children.curiosity: The Perceptron was the basis of the first hopes of AI in the 1950s-60s. Minsky and Papert showed its limitations in 1969 with the XOR problem.

children.name: Logistic Regression
children.diff_siblings: Linear classifier that models log-odds — differs from Perceptron by providing calibrated probabilities; from SGD by having a solution via convex optimization
weaknesses: Inferior performance to Gradient Boosting on complex data
not_recommended_for: Complex non-linear relationships
children.curiosity: Logistic regression is the most regulated model in the world — banks in many countries are required by law to use interpretable models for credit decisions.

children.name: Perceptron
children.diff_siblings: The simplest linear classifier — updates weights only on errors; differs from Logistic by not providing probabilities; converges only if data is linearly separable
strengths: Converges to separating solution if data is linear
weaknesses: Does not converge if data is not linearly separable
not_recommended_for: Practical applications — Logistic or SVM are superior
children.curiosity: Frank Rosenblatt built the Perceptron Mark I in 1958. The New York Times reported that the Navy revealed 'the embryo of an electronic computer that will be able to walk, talk, see, write, and be self-aware'.

children.name: Passive-Aggressive Classifier
children.diff_siblings: Online learning: aggressively updates when wrong and passively when right — differs from Perceptron by having a margin; from SGD by having exact update per sample
not_recommended_for: Batch data where SGD is equivalent
children.curiosity: Crammer et al. proposed PA in 2006 motivated by real-time news classification. The name captures the duality: passive when correct, aggressive when wrong.

children.name: SGD Classifier
children.diff_siblings: Stochastic gradient descent with several loss functions — it is an optimization framework, not a model; the loss defines the model (hinge→linear SVM, log→Logistic)
strengths: Scales to datasets with n > millions
One API for linear SVM, Logistic, and Perceptron
weaknesses: Requires normalization and tuning of learning rate
recommended_for: Large datasets where exact solvers are slow
not_recommended_for: Small datasets — exact solvers converge faster
children.curiosity: Gradient descent was invented by Cauchy in 1847. The stochastic version was developed by Robbins and Monro in 1951. SGD unifies 200 years of mathematical history.

children.name: Instance-based
children.diff_siblings: Lazy learners that classify by voting of neighbors — differ from parametric models by not compressing data into parameters
not_recommended_for: Large datasets
High dimensionality
children.curiosity: Cover and Hart's (1967) proof: 1-NN has asymptotic error at most 2× the Bayes error — a parameterless algorithm is within a factor of 2 of the theoretical optimum.

children.name: K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN)
children.diff_siblings: Majority voting among the K nearest neighbors — K controls the bias-variance trade-off; differs from LVQ by not learning prototypes
strengths: K=1 memorizes; large K smooths boundaries
not_recommended_for: Datasets with n > 100k
High dimensionality (p > 20)
children.curiosity: Odd value of K avoids ties. The rule of thumb K=√n comes from empirical studies from the 1970s. Today, sklearn uses Ball-tree or KD-tree to reduce from O(n) to O(log n).

children.name: Radius Neighbors Classifier
children.diff_siblings: Voting of all neighbors within radius r — adapts the number of neighbors to local density; can return 'inconclusive' in regions without neighbors
strengths: Number of neighbors adapts to density
not_recommended_for: When prediction guarantee for all points is necessary
children.curiosity: Radius Neighbors is the historical predecessor of KNN — the idea of 'neighborhood by proximity' precedes the concept of 'K neighbors'.

children.name: Learning Vector Quantization (LVQ)
children.diff_siblings: Learns representative prototypes per class via competitive training — compresses data into prototypes; differs from KNN by not storing all data
strengths: Compresses data into prototypes — fast inference
Competitive performance with KNN using a fraction of the data
recommended_for: When KNN is too slow but complex boundaries are necessary
not_recommended_for: Small datasets where KNN is already fast
children.curiosity: Teuvo Kohonen developed LVQ in 1988 as a supervised extension of SOM. LVQ anticipated the idea of 'exemplar models' in cognitive psychology.

children.name: Kernel-based
children.diff_siblings: SVMs maximize separation margin — differ from linear methods by projecting into high-dimensional space via kernel; from Naive Bayes by not modeling distributions
strengths: Boundaries determined by subset of points
not_recommended_for: Big data — LightGBM/XGBoost are much faster
children.curiosity: The kernel trick was discovered by Aizermann in 1964, but only applied to SVMs by Boser, Guyon and Vapnik in 1992.

children.name: SVM — linear kernel
children.diff_siblings: Maximum margin hyperplane in original space — different from other kernels because it does not project into high dimension; equivalent to SGD with hinge loss
strengths: Efficient for high dimension (NLP with TF-IDF)
weaknesses: Probabilities via Platt scaling add overhead
recommended_for: Text classification, bioinformatics with pre-computed features
not_recommended_for: Non-linearly separable data — RBF
Very large datasets — SGD is faster
children.curiosity: For text, linear SVM and Naive Bayes have comparable performance, but SVM outperforms on larger datasets. Joachims (1998) developed SVM-Light for document collections.

children.name: SVM — RBF kernel
children.diff_siblings: Gaussian kernel — the most versatile; maps data to infinite dimensional space; captures arbitrary non-linearity; only 2 hyperparameters (C, γ)
weaknesses: C and γ require grid search
not_recommended_for: Very large datasets — LightGBM is much faster
children.curiosity: γ controls the 'radius of influence': high γ → overfitting; low γ → underfitting. Grid search in log-scale for C and γ is the standard approach.

children.name: SVM — polynomial kernel
children.diff_siblings: Polynomial kernel of degree d — differs from RBF by having specific polynomial boundaries; captures order d interactions between features
strengths: Good for data with specific order interactions
not_recommended_for: General data — RBF is more versatile
Degree > 4 due to instability
children.curiosity: Used in the postal digit reading system at AT&T Bell Labs in the 1990s — one of the first large-scale production ML systems.

children.name: SVM — sigmoid kernel
children.diff_siblings: Mimics single-layer neural networks via tanh — does not satisfy Mercer's condition for all parameters; performance generally inferior to RBF
weaknesses: Does not satisfy Mercer's condition — can cause instability
not_recommended_for: Practical problems — RBF is more stable
children.curiosity: The sigmoid kernel was proposed to approximate neural networks with SVMs in the 1990s. With the resurgence of Deep Learning, this motivation lost relevance.

children.name: Nu-SVC
children.diff_siblings: Alternative parameterization with ν ∈ (0,1) that directly controls the fraction of support vectors — more intuitive interpretation than the abstract C parameter
strengths: ν has direct interpretation: maximum fraction of errors
weaknesses: ν does not map directly to C
Performance equivalent to C-SVC with proper tuning
not_recommended_for: Pure performance — C-SVC with grid search is equivalent
children.curiosity: Schölkopf et al. proposed Nu-SVM in 2000 in response to the lack of interpretability of the C parameter.

children.name: Trees
children.diff_siblings: Recursively partition the feature space — differ from linear methods due to axis-parallel non-linear boundaries; from SVMs for being discrete; from probabilistic ones for not modeling distributions
weaknesses: Single tree is unstable and overfits
Ensembles solve instability but lose interpretability
not_recommended_for: Textual and image data
When smooth boundaries are needed
children.curiosity: The first computational tree was the CLS program by Hunt, Marin, and Stone in 1963 — inspired by medical diagnosis trees.

children.name: Decision Tree
children.diff_siblings: Single tree — more interpretable but less accurate than ensembles; base for all ensemble methods
weaknesses: Unstable: small changes change the tree
not_recommended_for: Competitive performance — Random Forest or XGBoost
children.curiosity: John Ross Quinlan said his goal was always to create an 'algorithm that a human would understand' — not just one that works.

children.name: CART
children.diff_siblings: Breiman et al. — uses Gini or residual variance, produces binary trees; supports regression besides classification
weaknesses: Gini may favor features with more unique values
not_recommended_for: Categorical features with many levels — C4.5 handles better
children.curiosity: Leo Breiman, Jerome Friedman, Richard Olshen, and Charles Stone published CART in 1984. Breiman later created Random Forest and Gradient Boosting.

children.name: ID3
children.diff_siblings: Uses Information Gain for split selection — only for classification; no pruning; favors features with more categories (selection bias)
strengths: Simple concept based on information theory
not_recommended_for: Practical applications — C4.5 or CART are superior
children.curiosity: Quinlan developed ID3 in 1986 trying to learn chess rules from human games. The name means 'Iterative Dichotomiser 3'.

children.name: C4.5 / C5.0
children.diff_siblings: Uses Gain Ratio to correct ID3 bias; supports continuous features, missing values, and pruning; C5.0 adds boosting and rules
recommended_for: When readable decision rules are needed
not_recommended_for: Integration with sklearn — CART is native
Regression — C4.5 is classification only
children.curiosity: C4.5 was elected the #1 ML/Data Mining algorithm by IEEE ICDM in 2006 in a poll with experts.

children.name: CHAID
children.diff_siblings: Chi-squared Automatic Interaction Detector — uses chi-square for splits; supports multi-way splits; standard in market research
not_recommended_for: Continuous features without discretization
Maximum performance — CART or ensemble
children.curiosity: Gordon Kass developed CHAID in 1980 for marketing analysis. The use of chi-square gives a familiar statistical interpretation for those coming from classical statistics.

children.name: Conditional Inference Tree
children.diff_siblings: Tree with hypothesis tests and correction for multiple tests — no variable selection bias; differs from CART by using non-parametric tests
recommended_for: Statistical inference where absence of bias is critical
not_recommended_for: Maximum performance in ML — CART with ensembles surpasses
children.curiosity: Hothorn, Hornik and Zeileis (2006) showed that CART and C4.5 have systematic selection bias that can invalidate inferences in scientific research.

children.name: Ensemble — Bagging
children.diff_siblings: Trains models on independent bootstrap samples — different from Boosting for being parallel; from Stacking for using the same base algorithm; reduces variance
strengths: Out-of-bag error is a free estimate
weaknesses: Less efficient than Boosting when bias is the problem
recommended_for: When variance is the main problem
not_recommended_for: When bias is the main problem — Boosting
children.curiosity: Leo Breiman invented Bagging in 1994. The insight: unstable trees benefit greatly from bagging — stable learners (linear regression) gain little.

children.name: Random Forest
children.diff_siblings: Bagging with random feature selection at each split — decorrelates the trees; reference Bagging ensemble
weaknesses: Slower than single tree for inference
Generally surpassed by Boosting in tabular benchmarks
recommended_for: Solid baseline for any tabular problem
not_recommended_for: Maximum performance — XGBoost/LightGBM tend to surpass
children.curiosity: Breiman published Random Forest in 2001 combining Bagging (1994) and Ho's Random Subspaces (1998). He never patented the algorithm — made it freely available.

children.name: Extra Trees (Extremely Randomized Trees)
children.diff_siblings: Randomizes both features and split thresholds — more random than RF; faster to train; sometimes more accurate
weaknesses: Less established than RF as a reference
recommended_for: When RF training time is a bottleneck
not_recommended_for: When boundary interpretability matters
Very small datasets
children.curiosity: Geurts, Ernst and Wehenkel proposed Extra Trees in 2006. The surprising result: completely randomizing thresholds often performs as well as RF.

children.name: Bagging Classifier
children.diff_siblings: Generic bagging with any base estimator — different from RF because it does not randomize features; works with SVM, KNN, etc.
weaknesses: No feature randomization — less decorrelation than RF
recommended_for: Bagging of SVMs or other non-tree estimators
not_recommended_for: When trees are the base — use RF or Extra Trees
children.curiosity: Breiman proposed Bagging in 1994 and demonstrated that the effect is greater for 'unstable' estimators (deep trees) than for 'stable' ones (linear regression).

children.name: Random Patches
children.diff_siblings: Random sample of both instances and features for each estimator — generalizes RF and Random Subspaces
weaknesses: Less popular and documented than RF
recommended_for: Very large datasets where instance subsampling is necessary
not_recommended_for: General use — RF is more convenient
children.curiosity: Louppe and Geurts proposed Random Patches in 2012, unifying RF, Random Subspaces, and Bagging into a common framework.

children.name: Random Subspaces
children.diff_siblings: Trains each estimator on a random subset of features without instance bootstrap — precursor to RF
recommended_for: High dimensionality where the subset of relevant features is unknown
not_recommended_for: Low-dimensional data
When RF is already available
children.curiosity: Tin Kam Ho proposed Random Subspaces in 1998 — before Breiman's Random Forest. Breiman incorporated the idea by combining it with instance bootstrap.

children.name: Ensemble — Boosting
children.diff_siblings: Trains models sequentially, each correcting the errors of the previous one — different from Bagging because it is sequential and reduces bias (not variance); dominant paradigm in tabular data
weaknesses: More prone to overfitting than Bagging with noisy data
recommended_for: Tabular data where maximum performance is necessary
not_recommended_for: Data with a lot of noise — Bagging is more robust
children.curiosity: Robert Schapire proved in 1990 that 'weak learners can be boosted to strong learners' — answering a theoretical question from 1988. The proof was theoretical; only in 1995 with AdaBoost did a practical algorithm emerge.

children.name: AdaBoost
children.diff_siblings: Pioneer of boosting — adjusts weights of misclassified samples; simpler than GBM because it uses sample weights instead of gradients; more sensitive to outliers
not_recommended_for: Noisy data — GBM/XGBoost are more robust
children.curiosity: Freund and Schapire received the Gödel Prize in 2003 for AdaBoost. Schapire said he was 'genuinely surprised' that it worked so well.

children.name: Gradient Boosting (GBM)
children.diff_siblings: Friedman (2001) — generalizes boosting as gradient optimization of an arbitrary loss function; theoretical basis for XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost
recommended_for: When understanding the mechanism is important
not_recommended_for: Maximum performance — XGBoost or LightGBM with the same basis
children.curiosity: Jerome Friedman published GBM in 2001. XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost are all optimized implementations of Friedman's GBM.

children.name: XGBoost
children.diff_siblings: Chen and Guestrin (2014) — L1/L2 regularization, column-wise parallelism, native missing values; 10× faster than classic GBM
weaknesses: Slower than LightGBM on very large datasets
recommended_for: Standard in Kaggle tabular data competitions
not_recommended_for: Datasets with > 1M rows — LightGBM is more efficient
children.curiosity: XGBoost was used in 17 of the 29 winning solutions in Kaggle competitions in 2015-2016. Tianqi Chen developed it as a personal PhD project.

children.name: LightGBM
children.diff_siblings: Microsoft (2017) — leaf-wise growth and GOSS/EFB; 20× faster than XGBoost on large datasets via different growth and gradient sampling
strengths: 20× faster than XGBoost on large data
weaknesses: More prone to overfitting on small datasets (leaf-wise)
Parameters with names different from the conventional ones
not_recommended_for: Small datasets (<10k) — leaf-wise growth overfits
children.curiosity: GOSS (Gradient-based One-Side Sampling) and EFB (Exclusive Feature Bundling) are the two technical innovations that few users know but make LightGBM so efficient.

children.name: CatBoost
children.diff_siblings: Yandex (2017) — native encoding of categorical features via ordered boosting; does not require manual encoding of categoricals; uses permutation to avoid target leakage
strengths: Best native handling of categorical features
Ordered boosting reduces overfitting due to target leakage
weaknesses: Smaller community and documentation in English
recommended_for: Data with many high-cardinality categorical features
not_recommended_for: Data without categorical features — XGBoost/LightGBM are faster
children.curiosity: CatBoost was developed by Yandex in 2017. The problem of target leakage in categorical encoding was widely ignored — the paper demonstrated that popular methods like mean encoding contaminate the training.

children.name: HistGradientBoosting (sklearn)
children.diff_siblings: GBM via histograms integrated into sklearn — no external dependencies; similar to LightGBM; native support for missing values and categorical features
strengths: Native in sklearn — no extra installation
Native support for missing values and categoricals
not_recommended_for: Maximum performance — XGBoost/LightGBM are superior
children.curiosity: sklearn implemented HistGradientBoosting in 2019 directly inspired by LightGBM. The goal: a native 'good enough GBM' to reduce the entry barrier.

children.name: NGBoost (probabilistic)
children.diff_siblings: Gradient boosting for full distributions — returns distribution instead of point; uses natural gradients for stable convergence
recommended_for: When prediction uncertainty is as important as the central point
not_recommended_for: Pure predictive performance — XGBoost/LightGBM are superior
children.curiosity: Duan et al. proposed NGBoost in 2019 at the Stanford ML Group. The insight: boosting can optimize the negative log-likelihood of distributions — enabling full probabilistic prediction.

children.name: Ensemble — Stacking / Voting
children.diff_siblings: Stacking combines heterogeneous models via a meta-model — different from Bagging by using different models; from Boosting by training in parallel; Voting is a simplification without a learned meta-model
strengths: Combines strengths of very different models
Meta-model learns when to trust each model
weaknesses: Risk of data leakage without correct out-of-fold
Much more complex to implement and maintain
recommended_for: Competitions where maximum performance is needed
not_recommended_for: Production where simplicity is needed
children.curiosity: David Wolpert formalized Stacking in 1992. The key: out-of-fold predictions to train the meta-model — without this, it overfits trivially.

children.name: Stacking Classifier
children.diff_siblings: Meta-model learns to combine predictions via cross-validation to avoid leakage — differs from Voting by using a learned meta-model
recommended_for: Competitions where every AUC point matters
not_recommended_for: When any individual model already performs adequately
children.curiosity: The winners of the Netflix Prize (2009) used stacking of 107 different algorithms for the $1M prize.

children.name: Blending
children.diff_siblings: Variation of Stacking with fixed holdout instead of cross-validation — simpler and faster, but more prone to overfitting on the holdout
weaknesses: Holdout reduces training data for base models
not_recommended_for: Small datasets where holdout impacts training
children.curiosity: Blending was popularized on Kaggle as a shortcut for Stacking. The distinction is technical but important: Stacking uses all training data; Blending uses only part.

children.name: Voting Classifier (hard/soft)
children.diff_siblings: Majority voting (hard) or average of probabilities (soft) — no learned meta-model; simpler than Stacking
strengths: Soft voting frequently outperforms hard voting
No risk of overfitting in the meta-model
weaknesses: Assumes equal weight for all models
not_recommended_for: When models have very different performance
Competitions
children.curiosity: Soft Voting is theoretically superior to Hard Voting: if A says 0.9 and B says 0.8, the soft vote correctly favors the positive class even if C says 0.1.

children.name: SuperLearner
children.diff_siblings: Meta-ensemble with a formal theoretical foundation (oracle inequality) — guarantees performance close to the optimal oracle; uses rigorous cross-validation
strengths: Oracle inequality — converges to the best convex combination
recommended_for: Causal inference and epidemiology where theoretical guarantees matter
not_recommended_for: Kaggle competitions — heuristic Stacking is more flexible
children.curiosity: Mark van der Laan and Sheryl Rose developed SuperLearner as part of the Targeted Learning framework. The 'oracle inequality' proves that SuperLearner performs almost as well as the best estimator in the library.

children.name: Rules
children.diff_siblings: Generate sets of if-then directly — differ from trees by creating rules without a hierarchical structure; more interpretable for business rules; less common in modern ML
weaknesses: Performance generally inferior to modern ensembles
recommended_for: Expert systems with explicit business rules
not_recommended_for: Maximum performance — GBM outperforms
When tree structure is more natural
children.curiosity: Decision rules have roots in expert systems from the 1970s. The transition from hand-crafted rules to learned rules was a milestone in the development of intelligent systems.

children.name: RIPPER (JRip)
children.diff_siblings: Repeated Incremental Pruning — learns a set of rules with pruning; more expressive than OneR because it uses multiple conditions; different from PART because it is not tree-based
strengths: Competitive performance for its level of complexity
not_recommended_for: Maximum performance — GBM vastly outperforms
children.curiosity: Cohen proposed RIPPER in 1995. It was used in network intrusion detection in the early 2000s, where auditable rules were a security requirement.

children.name: OneR
children.diff_siblings: A rule based on a single attribute — the most predictive; surprisingly competitive as a baseline in many datasets
weaknesses: Only one attribute — underestimates multivariate relationships
recommended_for: Interpretability baseline — what is the best single attribute?
not_recommended_for: Any practical application beyond a baseline
children.curiosity: Robert Holte proposed OneR in 1993 demonstrating that very simple rules often perform close to more complex algorithms on UCI datasets.

children.name: PART
children.diff_siblings: Generates rules via partial trees — extracts the best rule, removes covered instances and repeats; differs from C4.5 by extracting independent rules instead of post-processing the tree
strengths: Better performance than C4.5-rules in some cases
recommended_for: When independent rules are more interpretable than tree hierarchy
not_recommended_for: Maximum performance
children.curiosity: Frank and Witten proposed PART in 1998. The insight: extracting the best rule from the current tree is better than converting the whole tree into rules at once.

children.name: Decision Table
children.diff_siblings: Multidimensional lookup table — for each combination of attributes, stores the majority class; no hierarchy; covers the space exhaustively
strengths: Extremely interpretable as a reference table
Easy to implement and audit manually
recommended_for: Few categorical attributes with reference decision
not_recommended_for: More than 5-6 attributes — combinatorial explosion
children.curiosity: Ron Kohavi proposed Decision Tables in 1995 formalizing a common practice in business analysis. The contribution was showing how to learn the best projection of attributes.

children.name: 1.1.3 Time Series
children.diff_siblings: Models temporal dependencies — differs from regression by incorporating chronological order and autocorrelation; from spatial processes by having a single dimension of dependency
strengths: Captures seasonal patterns, trend, and autocorrelation
weaknesses: Violation of stationarity invalidates classical models
Exogenous events (pandemics, crises) break any historical model
not_recommended_for: Data without genuine temporal dependency — classical regression
children.curiosity: Modern time series theory dates back to Yule (1927) who introduced autoregressive processes to model sunspots.

children.name: Classics (ARMA/ARIMA)
children.diff_siblings: Linear models based on lags — differ from Smoothing by having a formal probabilistic foundation; from Volatility by modeling the mean not the variance
weaknesses: Inferior performance to modern ML on long series
not_recommended_for: Series with non-linearity or complex structure
children.curiosity: George Box and Gwilym Jenkins popularized the ARIMA methodology in 1970 — so influential that it is called the 'Box-Jenkins methodology'.

children.name: AR (AutoRegressive)
children.diff_siblings: Regression on own lags — differs from MA by using past values of the series (not past errors); from ARMA by not having a moving average component
recommended_for: Series with autocorrelation dominated by own lags
not_recommended_for: Series with MA component — ARMA
children.curiosity: George Yule proposed AR in 1927 modeling sunspots. The insight: a time series can be generated by a difference equation with random perturbation.

children.name: MA (Moving Average)
children.diff_siblings: Regression on past errors — differs from AR by using past innovations; always stationary; rarely used alone
weaknesses: Rarely used alone — combined in ARMA
recommended_for: Series with autocorrelation that decays abruptly in the ACF
not_recommended_for: Series with long-term autocorrelation — AR
children.curiosity: Herman Wold proved in 1938 that any stationary process can be represented as MA(∞) — foundation of the Box-Jenkins framework.

children.name: ARMA
children.diff_siblings: Combines AR and MA — theoretical basis for extensions; complete model for stationary series
not_recommended_for: Non-stationary series — ARIMA
children.curiosity: Peter Whittle developed ARMA in 1951. An AR(1) with MA(1) captures structures that a pure AR would need a very high order to approximate.

children.name: ARIMA
children.diff_siblings: Adds differencing I(d) to ARMA for non-stationarity — the 'I' in Integrated refers to the inverse operation of differencing
recommended_for: Series with linear or stochastic trend
not_recommended_for: Series with seasonality — SARIMA
children.curiosity: Box and Jenkins published ARIMA in 1970. The identification-estimation-diagnostic cycle was the first systematic framework for time series analysis.

children.name: SARIMA
children.diff_siblings: ARIMA with seasonal components (P,D,Q)×s — captures autocorrelation at seasonal lags; baseline for series with clear seasonality
strengths: Direct and natural extension of ARIMA
recommended_for: Monthly or quarterly series with annual seasonality
not_recommended_for: Multiple seasonalities — TBATS or Prophet
children.curiosity: SARIMA was included in the Box-Jenkins methodology in 1970. With only 6 parameters, it captures complex annual patterns — parsimony is the model's strength.

children.name: ARIMAX / SARIMAX
children.diff_siblings: ARIMA/SARIMA with exogenous variables — incorporates external predictors; differs from ARIMA by including covariates; allows Granger causality
weaknesses: Requires exogenous variables available in the forecast horizon
recommended_for: Demand forecasting with planned promotion information
not_recommended_for: When there are no reliable exogenous variables
children.curiosity: Box and Tiao (1975) introduced 'intervention' in time series to model the impact of exogenous events. Modern retail promoters use SARIMAX to isolate the effect of promotions from seasonal patterns.

children.name: VAR (Vector AutoRegression)
children.diff_siblings: Multivariate system where each series regresses on lags of all — differs from ARIMA by capturing interdependencies between multiple series; differs from SUR by modeling temporal dynamics
recommended_for: Macroeconomics: GDP, inflation, unemployment, interest rates
not_recommended_for: Many series (K > 10) — sparse VAR
children.curiosity: Christopher Sims developed VAR in 1980 as an alternative to Simultaneous Equations. Sims received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2011.

children.name: VARMA
children.diff_siblings: Multivariate extension of ARMA — rarely used in practice due to identification difficulties
recommended_for: Multivariate series with identifiable MA component
not_recommended_for: Practical applications — VAR with more lags is simpler
children.curiosity: Hannan and Deistler discussed the identification difficulties of VARMA extensively in the 1980s.

children.name: VECM
children.diff_siblings: Vector Error Correction Model — VAR in differences with error correction terms for cointegrated series; differs from VAR by modeling long-run relationships
strengths: Explicit separation of short and long-run dynamics
recommended_for: Interest rate parities, related commodity prices
not_recommended_for: Series without cointegration — VAR in differences
children.curiosity: Engle and Granger (Nobel 2003) developed cointegration and the error correction model in 1987.

children.name: Naive Forecast / Seasonal Naive
children.diff_siblings: Forecast = last observed value (Naive) or last value of the same season — minimum baseline that any model must outperform
strengths: Hard to outperform in high variability series
weaknesses: Ignores all temporal structure beyond the last point
not_recommended_for: Production
children.curiosity: Rob Hyndman includes Naive and Seasonal Naive as mandatory benchmarks. The rule: if your model does not outperform Seasonal Naive, it is not learning anything beyond the simplest seasonal pattern.

children.name: Croston (intermittent demand)
children.diff_siblings: For series with many zeros — models occurrence frequency and order size separately; specific for sparse demand
not_recommended_for: Series without frequent zeros — ETS or ARIMA
children.curiosity: John Croston proposed it in 1972 for aircraft spare parts planning. Despite documented bias, it is still widely used for its conceptual simplicity.

children.name: Exponential Smoothing
children.diff_siblings: Assigns exponentially decreasing weights — heuristic without order specification; different from ARIMA for being non-parametric; basis of probabilistic ETS
strengths: Basis of ETS with rigorous statistical foundation
weaknesses: Inferior performance to modern ML on long series
recommended_for: Demand and inventory forecasting at scale
not_recommended_for: Series with multiple complex seasonalities
children.curiosity: Robert Brown developed Exponential Smoothing in the 1950s for US Navy missile tracking — the first real-time adaptive forecasting algorithm.

children.name: Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES)
children.diff_siblings: Exponential weighted average without trend or seasonality — only one parameter α; great for stationary series
strengths: Fast and robust for stationary series
weaknesses: Does not capture trend or seasonality
not_recommended_for: Series with trend — Holt
Seasonal series — Holt-Winters
children.curiosity: SES can be rewritten as ARIMA(0,1,1) — showing that exponential smoothing and ARIMA are not completely separate approaches.

children.name: Holt's Linear Trend
children.diff_siblings: Adds trend component to SES — two parameters (α, β) control the update speed of level and trend
recommended_for: Series with linear trend and no seasonality
not_recommended_for: Seasonal series — Holt-Winters
children.curiosity: Charles Holt developed it in 1957, but the report remained obscure for decades. Formally published only in 2004 — 47 years after its creation.

children.name: Holt-Winters (Seasonal)
children.diff_siblings: Adds multiplicative or additive seasonal component to Holt — seasonal baseline in demand forecasting
recommended_for: Series with annual seasonality and trend
not_recommended_for: Multiple seasonalities — TBATS or Prophet
children.curiosity: Peter Winters extended Holt in 1960. Multiplicative seasonality is more appropriate: December sales of a growing company are higher not just because it is December, but because the company has grown.

children.name: ETS (Error, Trend, Seasonality)
children.diff_siblings: Probabilistic framework unifying all smoothing methods — automatically selects the best combination via AIC
weaknesses: Automatic selection may choose an inappropriate model
recommended_for: Automated forecasting at scale with calibrated intervals
not_recommended_for: Specific series where domain knowledge defines the model
children.curiosity: Hyndman et al. formalized ETS in 2002 unifying decades of smoothing methods. The same state space that generates predictions automatically generates prediction intervals.

children.name: BATS
children.diff_siblings: Box-Cox, ARMA errors, Trend, Seasonal — captures non-integer seasonality and multiple frequencies; more flexible than ETS
not_recommended_for: Single seasonality — ETS is simpler
children.curiosity: De Livera et al. proposed BATS in 2011 motivated by electricity data with simultaneous daily, weekly, and annual seasonality.

children.name: TBATS
children.diff_siblings: Trigonometric Seasonal BATS — uses Fourier series for seasonality; more efficient than BATS for long seasonalities
recommended_for: Energy data: daily + weekly + annual seasonality
not_recommended_for: Single seasonality — ETS is simpler and faster
children.curiosity: TBATS was developed as an extension of BATS. The use of Fourier was inspired by Harvey and Shephard (1993).

children.name: STL (Seasonal-Trend Decomposition)
children.diff_siblings: Decomposes into trend, seasonality, and remainder via LOESS — decomposition, not direct forecasting; robust to outliers
weaknesses: Decomposition, not forecasting — requires additional model for the remainder
not_recommended_for: Direct forecasting — TBATS or Prophet integrate decomposition and forecasting
children.curiosity: Cleveland et al. proposed STL in 1990. Robustness to outliers via LOESS is the central innovation — today it is the reference decomposition method for exploration.

children.name: Volatility (ARCH/GARCH)
children.diff_siblings: Capture conditional heteroskedasticity in financial series — model variance (not the mean) as a dynamic process; captures 'volatility clusters'
weaknesses: Application almost exclusive to financial data
not_recommended_for: Non-financial series
children.curiosity: Robert Engle developed ARCH in 1982 studying British inflation and received the Nobel Prize in Economics in 2003.

children.name: ARCH
children.diff_siblings: AutoRegressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity — conditional variance regressed on past errors; GARCH generalized it making it rarely used directly
strengths: Foundation for the entire GARCH family
not_recommended_for: Practical applications — GARCH(1,1)
children.curiosity: Engle developed ARCH in 1982. σ²ₜ = α₀ + α₁ε²ₜ₋₁ — today's variance depends on the squares of past errors.

children.name: GARCH
children.diff_siblings: Bollerslev (1986) — adds lagged variance to ARCH; GARCH(1,1) is equivalent to ARCH(∞); reference model for financial volatility
weaknesses: Symmetric — does not distinguish positive from negative shocks
not_recommended_for: Data with leverage effect — EGARCH or GJR-GARCH
children.curiosity: Tim Bollerslev proposed GARCH in 1986 as a PhD thesis supervised by Engle. Current variance depends on past errors AND on past variance itself.

children.name: EGARCH
children.diff_siblings: Exponential GARCH — Nelson (1991); log of variance; captures asymmetry: negative shocks increase volatility more than positive ones
strengths: Log ensures positive variance without constraints
recommended_for: Stocks where drops increase volatility more than rises
not_recommended_for: Data without asymmetry — GARCH(1,1) is simpler
children.curiosity: Daniel Nelson proposed EGARCH in 1991. The 'leverage effect' was documented by Fischer Black in 1976: when the price falls, financial leverage increases and volatility grows more.

children.name: GJR-GARCH
children.diff_siblings: Glosten, Jagannathan and Runkle (1993) — adds asymmetric term for negative returns; more intuitive than EGARCH in parametrization
weaknesses: May underperform EGARCH in strong asymmetry
recommended_for: Financial data with moderate to strong asymmetry
not_recommended_for: Data without asymmetry — GARCH(1,1)
children.curiosity: GJR-GARCH was published in the Journal of Finance in 1993. The authors were testing whether expected return was positively related to risk — and accidentally created one of the most used volatility models.

children.name: ML / DL for Time Series
children.diff_siblings: Modern models — differ from classics by not assuming linearity; scale better for multiple series; foundation models work zero-shot
strengths: Scale to forecasting thousands of series
weaknesses: Require more data than classical models
not_recommended_for: Individual series where ARIMA/ETS are sufficient
children.curiosity: The revolution started with LSTM in the 2010s. The real leap came with foundation models (Chronos, TimeGPT) in 2023-2024 — pre-trained on billions of points that work zero-shot.

children.name: Prophet (Meta)
children.diff_siblings: Additive model with trend, seasonality and holidays — easier to use than ARIMA; uses Bayesian regression for the components
strengths: Handles holidays and special events natively
Robust to missing data and outliers
weaknesses: Inferior performance to LightGBM with external features
recommended_for: Forecasting series with seasonalities and holidays
not_recommended_for: When maximum performance is needed — TFT outperforms
children.curiosity: Taylor and Letham (Meta) published Prophet in 2018. Explicit goal: 'forecasting at scale for analysts who are not time series experts'.

children.name: Theta Model
children.diff_siblings: Winner of the M3 Competition (2000) — ensemble of two components: linear (long-term trend) and SES; surprisingly effective
not_recommended_for: Series with complex seasonality
children.curiosity: Assimakopoulos and Nikolopoulos proposed Theta in 2000 — the unlikely winner. It is technically equivalent to SES with drift under specific conditions.

children.name: N-BEATS
children.diff_siblings: Neural Basis Expansion Analysis — pure neural network without explicit time series components; won the M4 Competition
weaknesses: Requires more data than classical models
Less efficient than Transformers for long series
not_recommended_for: Multivariate series
Very short series
children.curiosity: Boris Oreshkin et al. published N-BEATS in 2020. A simple neural network of MLPs, without any time series inductive bias, outperformed all classical methods in the M4 Competition.

children.name: N-HiTS
children.diff_siblings: Neural Hierarchical Interpolation — extension of N-BEATS with multi-scale hierarchical interpolation; more efficient on long horizons
strengths: More efficient than N-BEATS on long horizons
Multi-scale captures long and short-term trends
not_recommended_for: Short horizons — N-BEATS or classical methods
children.curiosity: Challu et al. (Nixtla) published N-HiTS in 2022. The interpolation hierarchy was inspired by image pyramids in computer vision.

children.name: NNAR (Neural Network AutoRegression)
children.diff_siblings: MLP with series lags as inputs — different from LSTM for not having recurrent state; from N-BEATS for using lags as features
recommended_for: Series with moderate non-linearity in R
not_recommended_for: High performance — N-BEATS or TFT outperform
children.curiosity: Hyndman included NNAR in the forecast package in 2012. The NNAR(p,k) notation is analogous to ARIMA: p input lags, k neurons in the hidden layer.

children.name: TFT (Temporal Fusion Transformer)
children.diff_siblings: Transformer with interpretable temporal attention — mixes static, known-in-the-future, and historical variables; captures feature and lag importance
strengths: Mixes static, known-in-the-future, and historical variables
recommended_for: Multivariate forecasting with known future features
not_recommended_for: Simple univariate series — Prophet is sufficient
children.curiosity: Bryan Lim et al. (Google DeepMind) published TFT in 2021. The 'Variable Selection Networks' mechanism was created specifically for the time series problem.

children.name: Chronos (Amazon)
children.diff_siblings: Foundation model — pre-trained on billions of real and synthetic points; works zero-shot on any series; based on T5
weaknesses: No covariate incorporation in the base version
recommended_for: Fast forecasting of new series without training history
not_recommended_for: Series with many relevant covariates — TFT
children.curiosity: Ansari et al. (Amazon) published Chronos in 2024: tokenizing time series as text and pre-training a Transformer — the same paradigm that revolutionized NLP.

children.name: TimeGPT
children.diff_siblings: Nixtla foundation model — pre-trained on 100 billion points; offered as API; zero-shot and fine-tuning available
strengths: Pre-trained on the largest collection of public series
not_recommended_for: When full model control is required (regulation, privacy)
children.curiosity: Garza and Mergenthaler-Canseco (Nixtla) published TimeGPT in 2023. The paper showed that zero-shot TimeGPT outperforms specific models in more than half of the benchmarks.

children.name: Hierarchical Forecasting (reconciliation)
children.diff_siblings: Reconciliation of forecasts in hierarchical structure — ensures coherence between levels; top-down, bottom-up, and optimal approaches
strengths: Optimal reconciliation (MinT) uses information from all levels
weaknesses: Requires modeling and reconciliation — doubles the effort
