recommended_for: Demand forecasting in supply chains with geographic hierarchy
not_recommended_for: Series without genuine hierarchical structure
children.curiosity: Rob Hyndman developed the modern framework with MinT (Minimum Trace) in 2019. Reconciling projections using the error covariance matrix is optimal in the minimum variance sense.

children.name: State Space
children.diff_siblings: Represent system dynamics with latent state — more general than ARIMA; naturally support missing data; Kalman is the central algorithm
weaknesses: More complex to specify than ARIMA
not_recommended_for: Simple series where ARIMA is sufficient
children.curiosity: Rudolf Kalman published the filter in 1960 — originally for missile control engineering. The same algorithm that navigated the Apollo missions is used today in smartphones for sensor fusion.

children.name: Kalman Filter
children.diff_siblings: Optimal recursive estimation in linear-Gaussian systems — differs from HMM by having continuous states; updates prediction as data arrives
not_recommended_for: Non-linear systems — EKF/UKF/Particle Filter
children.curiosity: The Apollo 11 mission used the Kalman Filter implemented in Assembly with 4KB of memory — one of the first embedded ML applications in history.

children.name: Hidden Markov Model (HMM)
children.diff_siblings: Hidden discrete states with conditionally independent observations — differs from Kalman by having discrete states; wide application in speech and bioinformatics
strengths: Viterbi algorithm for most likely sequence
weaknesses: Assumes conditional independence of observations given the state
not_recommended_for: Sequences with dependence given the state — ARHMM
children.curiosity: Baum and Welch developed the training algorithm in 1966. For decades, HMMs dominated speech recognition — replaced by RNNs and Transformers in the 2010s.

children.name: Structural Time Series (STS)
children.diff_siblings: Decomposes series into interpretable components via state space — probabilistic, different from STL; explicit structural components with Bayesian estimation
recommended_for: Public policy data with identifiable interventions
not_recommended_for: Simple series where ARIMA is sufficient
children.curiosity: Harvey published the framework in 1989. Scott and Varian (Google) popularized it with the CausalImpact package (2015) for analyzing interventions in marketing campaigns.

children.name: Dynamic Linear Models (DLM)
children.diff_siblings: Time-varying coefficients — generalizes the Kalman filter; includes ARIMA, exponential smoothing, and STS as special cases
recommended_for: Regression with time-varying coefficients (e.g., variable asset beta)
not_recommended_for: Stable coefficients — classical regression
children.curiosity: West and Harrison published the seminal book on DLM in 1989. The connection between DLM and exponential smoothing provided a Bayesian foundation for empirical practices of decades.

children.name: 1.1.4 Survival (Survival Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: Modeling time-to-event with censored data — differs from regression by handling censoring; from classification by modeling when (not just if) the event occurs
strengths: Models both time and survival probability
Hazard ratio has causal interpretation in controlled studies
weaknesses: Requires assumption of independence between censoring and event
Extrapolation beyond observed data is risky
not_recommended_for: Events without censoring where classical regression is sufficient
children.curiosity: Kaplan and Meier (1958) — the most cited paper in JASA history with over 60,000 citations. It continues to be cited more than ever.

children.name: Kaplan-Meier
children.diff_siblings: Non-parametric estimator of the survival curve — no covariates; visualization and comparison of groups via log-rank test
weaknesses: Only group comparison — no adjustment for covariates
recommended_for: Visualization and comparison of survival curves
not_recommended_for: When adjustment for covariates is necessary — Cox PH
children.curiosity: Kaplan and Meier published in 1958. The paper solves how to estimate survival when some patients leave the study before the event — a fundamental and practical question.

children.name: Cox Proportional Hazards
children.diff_siblings: Semi-parametric model for conditional hazard — does not specify the baseline hazard shape; the most used in clinical studies
strengths: Semi-parametric — does not specify baseline hazard
Interpretable and widely accepted hazard ratio
not_recommended_for: When proportional hazards assumption is violated — AFT
children.curiosity: David Cox published in 1972 in just 12 pages — one of the most impactful contributions of 20th-century statistics.

children.name: Weibull Regression
children.diff_siblings: Parametric model — parametric form allows extrapolation; shape parameter interprets acceleration or deceleration of the hazard
recommended_for: Reliability engineering where extrapolation is necessary
not_recommended_for: Clinical studies where Cox is the standard
children.curiosity: Waloddi Weibull introduced the distribution in 1951 to model mechanical failures. The flexible shape makes it universal in reliability engineering.

children.name: AFT (Accelerated Failure Time)
children.diff_siblings: Models the log of survival time — coefficients interpreted as 'acceleration' of time; differs from Cox by scaling time instead of the hazard
strengths: Robust to violation of proportional hazards
weaknesses: Less established than Cox in clinical studies
recommended_for: When time interpretation is more intuitive than hazard
not_recommended_for: Clinical studies where reviewers expect hazard ratio
children.curiosity: 'Treatment B accelerates failure by 2×' is more understandable to non-statisticians than 'the hazard ratio is 2'.

children.name: Fine-Gray (competing risks)
children.diff_siblings: For competing events (death from specific cause vs. others) — correctly models the cumulative incidence function when there are competing risks
strengths: Correct modeling when competing events exist
recommended_for: Oncology: death from cancer vs. death from other causes
not_recommended_for: Single event — Cox is simpler
children.curiosity: Fine and Gray published in 1999. Kaplan-Meier overestimates the risk of death from cancer by treating other causes as censoring — Fine-Gray corrects this bias.

children.name: Random Survival Forest
children.diff_siblings: Extension of RF for survival data — non-parametric, non-linear; no assumption of proportional hazards
strengths: Captures interactions and non-linearity that Cox cannot
recommended_for: Churn prediction with many features and non-linear relationships
not_recommended_for: Clinical studies where hazard ratio is a regulatory requirement
children.curiosity: Ishwaran et al. developed RSF in 2008. The split criterion uses log-rank test instead of Gini impurity. RSF outperformed Cox in 15 bioinformatics datasets.

children.name: DeepSurv
children.diff_siblings: Neural network that extends the Cox model — uses MLP for the hazard function; training via backpropagation; captures non-linearity
weaknesses: Assumption of proportional hazards still present
recommended_for: Large survival datasets with complex features
not_recommended_for: Small datasets — Cox is more robust
children.curiosity: Katzman et al. (2018) elegantly: the Cox model can be written as a differentiable log-likelihood — just substitute the linear term with an MLP.

children.name: 1.2 Unsupervised
children.diff_siblings: Learns structure without labels — differs from Supervised by having no ground truth; from Semi-supervised by using no labels; discovers latent patterns
not_recommended_for: When labels are available — supervised performs better
children.curiosity: The first computational clustering algorithm, K-Means, was developed by Lloyd in 1957 at Bell Labs for signal quantization.

children.name: 1.2.1 Clustering
children.diff_siblings: Groups similar observations — differs from Dimensionality by assigning discrete memberships; from Anomalies by focusing on what is normal
not_recommended_for: When groups are known — classification
children.curiosity: 'The clustering curse': every algorithm finds clusters in random data. The statistical validation that clusters are 'real' remains an open problem.

children.name: Centroid
children.diff_siblings: Represents each cluster by centroid — assumes convex clusters; fast and scalable
not_recommended_for: Arbitrarily shaped clusters — DBSCAN
children.curiosity: K-Means was rediscovered by MacQueen (1967), who coined the name, and by Forgy (1965). Independent convergence suggests the solution has mathematical naturalness.

children.name: K-Means
children.diff_siblings: Minimizes intra-cluster inertia via iteration — differs from K-Means++ by having random initialization; from K-Medoids by using centroid (not real point)
weaknesses: Assumes spherical clusters of similar size
not_recommended_for: Non-convex clusters — DBSCAN
Data with outliers — K-Medoids
children.curiosity: The standard K-Means algorithm (Lloyd, 1957) was only formally published in 1982 — 25 years after its creation.

children.name: K-Means++
children.diff_siblings: K-Means with smart initialization — chooses initial centroid distant from those already chosen; O(log K) approximation to global optimum
recommended_for: Direct replacement for K-Means in any application
not_recommended_for: When standard K-Means is already sufficient
children.curiosity: Arthur and Vassilvitskii proposed K-Means++ in 2007 with guarantee: O(log K) times the optimal cost. Convergence in 3-10× fewer iterations than random K-Means.

children.name: K-Medoids (PAM)
children.diff_siblings: Uses real points as representatives — more robust to outliers; works with any metric; differs from K-Means by using a real point, not an artificial centroid
recommended_for: When interpretability of the representative is important
not_recommended_for: Large datasets — K-Means is orders of magnitude faster
children.curiosity: PAM (Partitioning Around Medoids) was proposed by Kaufman and Rousseeuw in 1987. In gene expression analysis, the medoid is literally the most 'typical' gene in the cluster.

children.name: Mini-Batch K-Means
children.diff_siblings: K-Means with random mini-batches — much faster, slightly less accurate; supports online learning
recommended_for: Datasets with more than 1 million points
not_recommended_for: Moderate datasets where K-Means is fast
children.curiosity: Sculley proposed it in 2010 motivated by clustering search queries at Google — billions of queries that don't fit in memory.

children.name: K-Medians
children.diff_siblings: Uses component-wise median — more robust to outliers than K-Means; representative may not be a real point
strengths: More robust to outliers than K-Means
Median is less sensitive to extreme values
weaknesses: Representative may not be a real point
recommended_for: Data with moderate outliers where K-Medoids is slow
not_recommended_for: Severe outliers — K-Medoids
When a real representative is needed
children.curiosity: K-Medians implicitly uses L1 norm — minimizes sum of absolute distances instead of K-Means' L2 norm. This mathematical difference is the reason for the robustness.

children.name: Fuzzy C-Means
children.diff_siblings: Fuzzy clustering with degree of membership to each cluster — differs from K-Means by partial (soft) assignment; from GMM by not being probabilistic
recommended_for: Text analysis with documents on multiple topics
not_recommended_for: Discrete clusters are needed — K-Means
Probabilistic foundation — GMM
children.curiosity: Dunn proposed FCM in 1973. In MRI medical image segmentation, pixels on the border between tissues have genuinely partial membership.

children.name: Density-based
children.diff_siblings: Defines clusters as high-density regions separated by low density — no K a priori; detects outliers as noise; non-spherical shape
weaknesses: Sensitive to parameters ε and minPts
not_recommended_for: High dimensionality
Approximately spherical clusters — K-Means
children.curiosity: DBSCAN won the Test of Time Award at KDD 2014 — 18 years after its creation. The intuition of 'density' as a criterion is more natural than 'centroid' for many physical phenomena.

children.name: DBSCAN
children.diff_siblings: Expands clusters from core points with sufficient density — parameters ε and minPts; classifies points as core, border, or noise
not_recommended_for: High dimensionality without prior reduction
Clusters with very different densities — HDBSCAN
children.curiosity: Ester, Kriegel, Sander, and Xu proposed DBSCAN in 1996. The parameter ε can be estimated via the k-distance graph.

children.name: HDBSCAN
children.diff_siblings: Density hierarchy — no fixed ε; extracts stable clusters at different scales; detects clusters with varying densities
strengths: Less sensitive to parameters than DBSCAN
not_recommended_for: Very large datasets with homogeneous density — DBSCAN
children.curiosity: Campello, Moulavi, and Sander proposed HDBSCAN in 2013, solving DBSCAN's main practical problem: real clusters rarely have the same density.

children.name: OPTICS
children.diff_siblings: Ordering Points To Identify Clustering Structure — produces reachability plot; solves DBSCAN's single ε problem
not_recommended_for: Production where defined clusters are needed — HDBSCAN
children.curiosity: Ankerst et al. proposed OPTICS in 1999. The reachability plot allows seeing how many clusters exist at different scales without running DBSCAN multiple times.

children.name: Mean Shift
children.diff_siblings: Iterates towards the local density maximum via kernel estimation — no K a priori; converges to distribution modes
not_recommended_for: Large datasets — quadratic cost
children.curiosity: Fukunaga and Hostetler proposed Mean Shift in 1975. Comaniciu and Meer popularized it for image segmentation in 2002.

children.name: Hierarchical
children.diff_siblings: Builds dendrogram — no K a priori; shows nested structure; K can be chosen after construction
strengths: K can be chosen after construction
weaknesses: O(n² log n) — does not scale to big data
Choice of linkage strongly affects the result
recommended_for: Small datasets where dendrogram is feasible
not_recommended_for: Large datasets — K-Means
children.curiosity: The dendrogram was used in biological taxonomy. The computational version was developed by Ward in 1963 to group municipalities by socioeconomic characteristics.

children.name: Agglomerative (Ward, Complete, Average, Single)
children.diff_siblings: Bottom-up — each point starts as a cluster; Ward minimizes intra-cluster variance; Single-link is susceptible to chaining
strengths: Ward is equivalent to hierarchical K-Means
weaknesses: O(n² log n) — does not scale
not_recommended_for: Big data
When hierarchy does not exist in the data
children.curiosity: Ward proposed the minimum variance criterion in 1963. Ward produces more compact and similarly sized clusters — behavior closer to K-Means, with the benefit of the dendrogram.

children.name: BIRCH (Balanced Iterative Reducing and Clustering)
children.diff_siblings: Scalable via CF-tree (Clustering Feature tree) — different from Agglomerative for scaling via summarization; does not produce a complete dendrogram
recommended_for: Large datasets where Agglomerative does not fit in memory
not_recommended_for: Non-convex clusters — DBSCAN
children.curiosity: Zhang, Ramakrishnan, and Livny proposed BIRCH in 1996 — one of the first ML algorithms designed for scalability.

children.name: Divisive Clustering
children.diff_siblings: Top-down — starts with all points in one cluster and splits recursively; different from Agglomerative for being top-down
strengths: Can use K-Means for efficient splitting
weaknesses: O(2^n) for exact splitting — unfeasible without heuristics
recommended_for: When high-level structure is more important
not_recommended_for: Big data
children.curiosity: Bisecting K-Means — scalable version of Divisive — was proposed by Steinbach et al. in 2000 for large document collections.

children.name: Probabilistic / Mixture Models
children.diff_siblings: Models data as a mixture of distributions — soft (probabilistic) assignment; generative foundation; K selection via AIC/BIC
weaknesses: Requires specification of the distribution family
EM can converge to local maxima
not_recommended_for: Purely deterministic clusters — K-Means
children.curiosity: The EM algorithm (Dempster, Laird, and Rubin, 1977) is the heart of all mixture models — one of the most cited papers in the history of statistics.

children.name: GMM (Gaussian Mixture Model)
children.diff_siblings: Mixture of Gaussians with estimation via EM — elliptical clusters of any orientation; differs from K-Means due to soft assignment and from K-Medoids for being probabilistic
not_recommended_for: Unknown K — Dirichlet GMM
Very irregular clusters — DBSCAN
children.curiosity: GMM applied to clustering is technically different from GMM as a density model — but mathematically identical.

children.name: Dirichlet Process GMM (DPGMM)
children.diff_siblings: Non-parametric GMM that learns the number of components — uses Dirichlet Process as prior; number of clusters grows with data
strengths: Naturally adds new clusters for new data
weaknesses: Concentration parameter α controls number of clusters
recommended_for: When K is genuinely unknown and data is abundant
not_recommended_for: When K is approximately known — GMM with BIC
children.curiosity: Ferguson developed the Dirichlet Process in 1973. The 'Chinese Restaurant Process' — metaphor for the DP — is one of the most elegant probabilistic constructions in ML.

children.name: LDA Topics (Latent Dirichlet Allocation)
children.diff_siblings: Generative model for document collections — each document is a mixture of topics, each topic is a distribution of words; differs from GMM by being discrete
recommended_for: Thematic analysis of large text corpora
not_recommended_for: Short text (tweets) — sparse words
When semantics needs to capture order — BERT
children.curiosity: Blei, Ng, and Jordan proposed LDA in 2003 — one of the most cited papers in ML with over 50,000 citations.

children.name: NMF (Non-negative Matrix Factorization)
children.diff_siblings: Factorization with non-negativity constraint — parts-based; differs from PCA by non-negative factors; from LDA by not being probabilistic
weaknesses: Number of components R requires specification
not_recommended_for: Data with negative values — PCA
Probabilistic interpretation — LDA
children.curiosity: Lee and Seung published NMF in Nature in 1999. PCA produced holistic components; NMF produced local components (nose, eyes, mouth) — more aligned with human perception.

children.name: Graph-based
children.diff_siblings: Represents data as a graph and finds clusters via cut — differs from centroid by using topology; from density by operating on explicit graph
weaknesses: Scales poorly with n — adjacency matrices are O(n²)
recommended_for: Manifold clustering with complex topological structure
not_recommended_for: Big data — graph cost is prohibitive
children.curiosity: Spectral Clustering and SOM converge to the idea that data geometry should guide clustering — perspective that anticipated TDA (Topological Data Analysis).

children.name: Spectral Clustering
children.diff_siblings: Uses eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian matrix — discovers non-convex clusters via normalized cut; differs from K-Means by operating in spectral geometry
strengths: Solid theoretical foundation in graph cut
not_recommended_for: Data with convex clusters — K-Means
children.curiosity: Shi and Malik proposed Normalized Cuts in 2000 for image segmentation. Ng, Jordan, and Weiss formalized Spectral Clustering for general data in 2001.

children.name: Affinity Propagation
children.diff_siblings: Exchanges messages of 'responsibility' and 'availability' — identifies actual exemplars without a priori K; based on message passing
strengths: Identifies actual exemplars without a priori K
Messages converge to a coherent solution
weaknesses: Preference parameter controls number of clusters
recommended_for: Medium datasets (<10k) without a priori K
not_recommended_for: Big data — quadratic cost
children.curiosity: Frey and Dueck published in Science in 2007 — one of the few ML papers published in Science. The mechanism was inspired by belief propagation from belief networks.

children.name: SOM (Self-Organizing Map)
children.diff_siblings: Competitive neural network that learns a topologically ordered 2D map — preserves topology; different from K-Means because it has a discrete grid representation
weaknesses: Fixed grid may not represent real topology
recommended_for: Visualization and exploratory analysis of high dimension
not_recommended_for: When precise clusters are needed — K-Means
children.curiosity: Teuvo Kohonen developed SOM in 1982 inspired by topographic maps of the cerebral cortex. The brain organizes sensory information in 2D maps — SOM is a computational abstraction of this organization.

children.name: 1.2.2 Dimensionality Reduction
children.diff_siblings: Projects high-dimensional data into a smaller representation — differs from Clustering by producing continuous coordinates; from Feature Selection by creating new features
weaknesses: New dimensions may not be interpretable
recommended_for: Preprocessing for models with curse of dimensionality
not_recommended_for: When original features are interpretable and necessary
children.curiosity: Harold Hotelling developed PCA in 1933. The 'curse of dimensionality' — Bellman, 1957 — motivated decades of research in dimensionality reduction.

children.name: Linear
children.diff_siblings: Linear projection — differs from non-linear methods by preserving only linear structure; much more computationally efficient
weaknesses: Does not capture non-linear structure (curved manifolds)
recommended_for: Data that varies in a linear subspace
not_recommended_for: Data on non-linear manifold — t-SNE or UMAP
children.curiosity: The SVD decomposition — heart of PCA — was developed by Beltrami in 1873 and Jordan in 1874. The 150-year-old theory is implemented in every modern linear algebra library.

children.name: PCA (Principal Component Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: Finds directions of maximum variance via SVD — differs from ICA by maximizing variance (not independence); from Factor Analysis by not having an explicit error model
weaknesses: Maximum variance does not imply relevance for the task
recommended_for: Removal of correlation before linear models
not_recommended_for: Non-linear data — UMAP
Original features needed — feature selection
children.curiosity: PCA was developed by Pearson (1901) and Hotelling (1933). The 'loadings' are the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix — connection with quantum mechanics where stationary states are also eigenvectors.

children.name: ICA (Independent Component Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: Finds statistically independent components (not just uncorrelated) — for source separation (BSS); differs from PCA by maximizing independence
recommended_for: Removal of artifacts from biological signals
not_recommended_for: Gaussian data — PCA and ICA are equivalent
children.curiosity: ICA was popularized by Bell and Sejnowski in 1995 for the 'cocktail party problem': separating voice from multiple people using mixed microphones.

children.name: SVD (Singular Value Decomposition)
children.diff_siblings: Factorization A = UΣVᵀ — mathematical basis of PCA; differs from PCA by operating on the data matrix directly; used in LSA and recommendation systems
strengths: Basis of LSA, PCA and many others
weaknesses: O(min(mn², m²n)) — slow for large matrices
not_recommended_for: Independent components needed — ICA
children.curiosity: SVD was developed by Beltrami and Jordan in the 1870s. The application in image compression in the 1980s was the first embedded ML application: digital cameras used truncated SVD.

children.name: Factor Analysis
children.diff_siblings: Models correlations via common latent factors plus specific error — differs from PCA by having a probabilistic model with error; origins in psychometrics
strengths: Separation between common and specific variance
not_recommended_for: Pure compression — PCA is simpler
children.curiosity: Charles Spearman developed Factor Analysis in 1904 trying to prove the 'g' factor of intelligence. The model is still the basis of all IQ tests.

children.name: Random Projections
children.diff_siblings: Projects into random subspace via Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma — O(1) to build projection; JL guarantees distance preservation with high probability
weaknesses: More dimensions needed for same precision as PCA
not_recommended_for: Moderate dimensionality where PCA is computationally feasible
children.curiosity: The Johnson-Lindenstrauss Lemma (1984): n points in R^d can be projected into R^k (k = O(log n / ε²)) preserving distances with error ε.

children.name: Non-Linear (Manifold Learning)
children.diff_siblings: Learns non-linear structure assuming data reside on low-dimensional manifold — different from linear methods by capturing curvature
strengths: Captures non-linear structure and curved manifolds
2D visualizations much more informative than PCA
weaknesses: Computationally much more expensive than PCA
Does not provide projection for new points
recommended_for: Visualization of text and image embeddings
not_recommended_for: Data in linear subspace — PCA is faster
children.curiosity: Isomap, LLE and Laplacian Eigenmaps were published in the same period (2000-2003) — the 'manifold learning boom'.

children.name: t-SNE
children.diff_siblings: Reduces high-dimensional distances to probabilities and minimizes KL-divergence — different from UMAP for having a more rigorous probabilistic basis; clusters very well separated visually
strengths: Preserves local structure with high fidelity
recommended_for: Visualization of word embeddings, images, biological cells
not_recommended_for: When global structure matters — UMAP
Large datasets — UMAP is 5-10× faster
children.curiosity: Van der Maaten and Hinton published t-SNE in 2008. The Student's t-distribution solves the 'crowding problem' — distant points in high dimension would be projected very close with a Gaussian.

children.name: UMAP
children.diff_siblings: Learns topological structure via Riemannian complex — preserves global structure better than t-SNE; faster; supports transform() for new points
weaknesses: Can create artificial structure in uniform data
recommended_for: Dimensionality reduction for ML pipelines (not only visualization)
not_recommended_for: Rigorous probabilistic basis — t-SNE
children.curiosity: McInnes et al. (2018) with foundation in algebraic topology. UMAP quickly surpassed t-SNE in single-cell genomics — where datasets of 1M+ cells are common.

children.name: Isomap
children.diff_siblings: Preserves geodesic distances on the manifold via MDS after graph construction — differs from PCA by using geodesic distances; from LLE by preserving global distances
strengths: Preserves global distances on the manifold
not_recommended_for: Manifolds with discontinuities — LLE
children.curiosity: Tenenbaum et al. published Isomap in Science in 2000 demonstrating that images of faces at different angles can be reduced to 2D preserving continuous variation.

children.name: LLE (Locally Linear Embedding)
children.diff_siblings: Preserves local linear reconstruction weights — each point reconstructed by linear combination of its neighbors; robust to manifolds with high curvature
recommended_for: Manifolds with high curvature where Isomap fails
not_recommended_for: Global structure — Isomap or UMAP
children.curiosity: Roweis and Saul published LLE in Science in 2000 — in the same issue as Isomap. The two papers launched the field of manifold learning.

children.name: Spectral Embedding
children.diff_siblings: Uses eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian — equivalent to Laplacian Eigenmaps; mathematical basis for Spectral Clustering
recommended_for: Spectral analysis of graphs and networks
not_recommended_for: Global structure — Isomap
Production where transform() is necessary — UMAP
children.curiosity: Belkin and Niyogi proposed Laplacian Eigenmaps in 2003. The discrete Laplacian on graphs is the computational version of the Laplace-Beltrami operator in differential geometry.

children.name: LTSA (Local Tangent Space Alignment)
children.diff_siblings: Estimates local tangent space and aligns globally — more accurate than LLE on smooth manifolds of low curvature
strengths: More accurate than LLE on smooth manifolds
weaknesses: Less popular than UMAP/t-SNE in practice
recommended_for: Smooth manifolds where tangent space is well-defined
not_recommended_for: Manifolds with high curvature — LLE
children.curiosity: Zhang and Zha proposed LTSA in 2004, part of the golden period of manifold learning (2000-2006).

children.name: MDS (Multidimensional Scaling)
children.diff_siblings: Preserves pairwise distances — linear case is equivalent to PCA; flexible for any distance or dissimilarity matrix
strengths: Classical MDS has analytical solution via SVD
weaknesses: Classical MDS is equivalent to PCA
recommended_for: Data defined by distances without explicit features
not_recommended_for: Data with explicit features — PCA is more efficient
children.curiosity: MDS was developed in psychology in the 1950s by Torgerson to map perceived similarity of stimuli. Given only the distances between US cities, MDS reconstructs the geographic map.

children.name: 1.2.3 Anomaly Detection
children.diff_siblings: Identifies observations that deviate from the normal pattern — differs from clustering by focusing on outliers; from classification by not having anomaly labels
strengths: Generic — any deviation from the pattern
weaknesses: High false positive rate in noisy data
'Normal' is hard to define in complex data
not_recommended_for: Anomalies with specific pattern — supervised classification
children.curiosity: Anomaly detection originates in Shewhart's statistical quality control in the 1920s — control charts identified points outside the ±3σ limits.

children.name: Isolation Forest
children.diff_siblings: Isolates anomalies via random partitions — anomalies isolated faster; different from LOF for being tree-based (faster); from One-Class SVM for being non-parametric
strengths: No critical parameters besides number of trees
weaknesses: Can fail on high density anomalies
not_recommended_for: Anomalies in clusters — LOF
children.curiosity: Liu, Ting and Zhou proposed Isolation Forest in 2008. The insight: instead of modeling normal behavior, it measures how easy it is to 'isolate' a point — anomalous points are isolated with fewer partitions.

children.name: LOF (Local Outlier Factor)
children.diff_siblings: Compares local density of a point with its neighbors — differs from Isolation Forest for being based on relative local density; detects local anomalies
strengths: Less sensitive to global density variations
recommended_for: Datasets with variable density where local anomalies matter
not_recommended_for: Big data — Isolation Forest is orders of magnitude faster
children.curiosity: Breunig et al. proposed LOF in 2000. A crime in a residential area is locally anomalous even if not statistically extreme globally.

children.name: One-Class SVM
children.diff_siblings: Learns a boundary around normal data in kernel space — different from LOF/Isolation Forest for being parametric and using kernel
weaknesses: Sensitive to kernel and parameter ν
recommended_for: Novelty detection with normal operation data
not_recommended_for: Big data — Isolation Forest is faster
children.curiosity: Schölkopf et al. proposed One-Class SVM in 2001. The kernel trick projects into a high-dimensional space where normal data are easier to separate from the rest.

children.name: Autoencoder for Anomalies
children.diff_siblings: Uses reconstruction error as score — trained on normal data has high error on anomalies; different from LOF/Isolation Forest for being deep learning
strengths: Captures complex normal patterns via DL
Works on images, text, and time series
weaknesses: Complex anomalies may not have high error
recommended_for: Anomalies in images, time series, and high dimension
not_recommended_for: Simple tabular data — Isolation Forest
children.curiosity: The use of autoencoders for anomalies emerged with applications in network intrusion detection in the 2010s. The principle: the autoencoder 'does not know' how to reconstruct anomalies.

children.name: 1.2.4 Representation
children.diff_siblings: Learns compact latent representations — different from dimensionality reduction for focusing on semantic quality; from clustering for producing continuous space; base for transfer learning
weaknesses: Quality difficult to evaluate without downstream task
not_recommended_for: When labels are available — supervised is more efficient
children.curiosity: Word2Vec (2013) inaugurated the modern era of embeddings — 'king - man + woman ≈ queen' encodes semantics in vector operations.

children.name: Word2Vec
children.diff_siblings: Word embeddings via Skip-gram or CBOW — different from GloVe for being based on local context window; from BERT for being static (one representation per word)
weaknesses: Replaced by BERT for most NLP tasks
not_recommended_for: NLP tasks where context matters — BERT
children.curiosity: Mikolov et al. (Google) published Word2Vec in 2013. The code was published in C with only 600 lines — one of the most impactful ML releases in history.

children.name: GloVe (Global Vectors)
children.diff_siblings: Factors global co-occurrence matrix — different from Word2Vec for using global co-occurrences; more efficient for large vocabularies
strengths: Less sensitive to hyperparameters than Word2Vec
recommended_for: When global co-occurrences are more informative than local window
not_recommended_for: Modern NLP tasks — BERT and derivatives are superior
children.curiosity: Pennington, Socher, and Manning (Stanford) published GloVe in 2014. The Word2Vec vs GloVe debate lasted years — with BERT in 2018, both were partially replaced.

children.name: FastText
children.diff_siblings: Subword-based embeddings (character n-grams) — different from Word2Vec because it handles out-of-vocabulary words via n-gram composition; better for morphologically rich languages
strengths: Better for languages with rich morphology (Portuguese)
weaknesses: Less popular than BERT in modern NLP
recommended_for: Portuguese and other languages with many morphological forms
not_recommended_for: Simple English where Word2Vec is sufficient
children.curiosity: Bojanowski et al. (FAIR/Meta) published FastText in 2016. For Portuguese, FastText is often superior to Word2Vec — Portuguese has rich morphology and subword treatment automatically captures relationships between 'correr', 'correndo', 'correção'.

children.name: 1.3 Semi-Supervised
children.diff_siblings: Uses few labeled data and many unlabeled data — differs from Supervised by leveraging unlabeled data; from Unsupervised by using some supervision signal
strengths: Leverages large volumes of unlabeled data
Often outperforms supervised with few labels
weaknesses: Unlabeled data can worsen the model if assumptions fail
recommended_for: NLP and vision where labeling is expensive but raw data is abundant
not_recommended_for: Data with many labels available — supervised is simpler
children.curiosity: Chapelle, Schölkopf and Zien edited 'Semi-Supervised Learning' in 2006. The central assumption (cluster assumption): data in the same cluster should have the same label.

children.name: Label Propagation
children.diff_siblings: Propagates labels through the similarity graph — different from Label Spreading by not having smoothing; from Self-Training by using a graph instead of iterative re-training
not_recommended_for: Data without clear graph structure
children.curiosity: Zhu and Ghahramani proposed Label Propagation in 2002. The solution is the harmonic function that interpolates known labels, preserving the graph structure.

children.name: Label Spreading
children.diff_siblings: Label Propagation with regularization — differs from Label Propagation by having parameter α that controls the balance between adherence to labels and smoothing
not_recommended_for: Reliable labels — Label Propagation without regularization
children.curiosity: Zhou et al. proposed Label Spreading in 2003 solving a problem with Label Propagation: if a label is wrong, it propagates the error uncontrollably.

children.name: Self-Training
children.diff_siblings: Trains a supervised model, classifies unlabeled data with high confidence and adds to training — iterative and simple; works with any classifier
not_recommended_for: When classification errors are frequent — propagates errors
children.curiosity: Yarowsky proposed Self-Training in 1995. GPT and modern language models use variants via pseudo-labels — the method was rediscovered multiple times.

children.name: Co-Training
children.diff_siblings: Trains two classifiers on different 'views' and uses predictions from one to label data of the other — exploits redundancy of multiple views
strengths: Two models correct each other mutually
weaknesses: Requires features naturally divisible into independent views
recommended_for: Problems with natural views: text + image
not_recommended_for: When features do not have a natural division into views — Self-Training
children.curiosity: Blum and Mitchell proposed Co-Training in 1998 for web page classification — page features and link features are two natural views.

children.name: Pseudo-Labels
children.diff_siblings: Uses high-confidence predictions as labels for unlabeled data — batch version of Self-Training; basis of modern SSL in deep learning
recommended_for: SSL in computer vision with DL
not_recommended_for: Small datasets where pseudo-label quality is low
children.curiosity: Lee proposed Pseudo-Labels in 2013. It is the basis of FixMatch, MixMatch and other modern SSL methods in computer vision.

children.name: TSVM (Transductive SVM)
children.diff_siblings: Extends SVM to classify unlabeled data maximizing joint margin — transductive; differs from SVM by including unlabeled points in optimization
recommended_for: When SVM foundation is necessary in a semi-supervised context
not_recommended_for: Big data — too slow
When prediction for new points is necessary
children.curiosity: Vapnik proposed TSVM in 1998. The transductive approach reflects a different philosophy: why learn a general function when the goal is to classify only a fixed set of points?

children.name: 1.4 Reinforcement Learning
children.diff_siblings: Agent learns by interacting with environment via rewards — differs from Supervised by having no labels; from Unsupervised by having explicit goal signal
weaknesses: Dense rewards are difficult to define
recommended_for: Games, robotics, process control, sequential recommendation
not_recommended_for: When demonstrations of optimal behavior are available
children.curiosity: Sutton and Barto developed the modern foundations of RL in the 1980s. AlphaGo (2016) and ChatGPT (via RLHF) brought RL to the mainstream.

children.name: Model-Free
children.diff_siblings: Learns policy directly from experience without environment model — simpler but less data efficient; different from Model-Based by not requiring transition model
strengths: No need to learn environment model
Converges to optimal policy with sufficient exploration
recommended_for: Environments with many cheap interactions (games, simulation)
not_recommended_for: Physical environments where interactions are expensive — Model-Based
children.curiosity: Q-Learning (Watkins, 1989) was the first model-free algorithm with convergence guarantees.

children.name: Q-Learning
children.diff_siblings: Learns Q(s,a) function via Bellman equation — off-policy; differs from SARSA by learning optimal Q independent of the exploration policy; basis of DQN
strengths: Off-policy — learns from data of any policy
Basis of all modern Deep RL
weaknesses: Q-table scales poorly with continuous states
recommended_for: Environments with discrete states and actions
not_recommended_for: Continuous spaces — DQN or SAC
children.curiosity: Chris Watkins proposed Q-Learning in 1989. DeepMind combined with neural networks to create DQN (2015), which played Atari at human level.

children.name: SARSA
children.diff_siblings: On-policy — updates Q(s,a) based on the action actually taken; differs from Q-Learning by being on-policy; more conservative in stochastic environments
strengths: On-policy — learns the policy actually followed
recommended_for: Process control where safety during learning matters
not_recommended_for: When data efficiency is a priority — Q-Learning off-policy
children.curiosity: SARSA: in 'cliff walking', Q-Learning learns to walk along the edge (optimal but falls during training); SARSA learns to stay away (safer).

children.name: DQN (Deep Q-Network)
children.diff_siblings: Combines Q-Learning with CNN — experience replay and target network stabilize training; first RL algorithm at human level in Atari
strengths: Experience replay and target network stabilize
weaknesses: Requires many samples — 50M frames per game
recommended_for: Environments with image observations and discrete actions
not_recommended_for: Continuous actions — SAC or DDPG
children.curiosity: Mnih et al. (DeepMind) published DQN in Nature in 2015. The system played 49 Atari games with the same architecture, learning only from pixels and score.

children.name: PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization)
children.diff_siblings: Policy optimization with change constraint via clipping — simpler and more scalable than TRPO; standard in RLHF for LLMs
not_recommended_for: When sample efficiency is critical — SAC off-policy
children.curiosity: Schulman et al. (OpenAI) proposed PPO in 2017. It became the standard at OpenAI for its combination of simplicity and robustness. Central to the development of ChatGPT via RLHF.

children.name: SAC (Soft Actor-Critic)
children.diff_siblings: Off-policy with entropy maximization — different from PPO by being off-policy; from DDPG by being more stable; standard in robotics with continuous actions
not_recommended_for: Discrete environments — DQN
When simplicity is a priority — PPO
children.curiosity: Haarnoja et al. (Berkeley) published SAC in 2018. Entropy maximization — training the agent to be 'random' while maximizing reward — was counterintuitive but produced more robust policies.

children.name: A3C/A2C
children.diff_siblings: Asynchronous Actor-Critic — different from PPO for using asynchronous gradients from multiple workers; from REINFORCE for having a critic (value baseline)
weaknesses: Instability with asynchronous gradients in A3C
Replaced by PPO in most applications
recommended_for: Environments that are very fast to simulate
not_recommended_for: Modern applications — PPO or SAC are superior
children.curiosity: Mnih et al. (DeepMind) proposed A3C in 2016. A2C (synchronous) proved to be more efficient than A3C in many cases — contrary to the intuition that more parallelism always helps.

children.name: TRPO (Trust Region Policy Optimization)
children.diff_siblings: Policy optimization with guarantee of monotonic improvement via KL-divergence constraint — different from PPO for being more mathematically rigorous; PPO was proposed as a practical simplification of TRPO
weaknesses: Much more complex to implement than PPO
Computes inverse Hessian via CG — computationally expensive
Replaced by PPO in most applications
recommended_for: Physical environments where policy collapse is dangerous
not_recommended_for: Practical applications — PPO is simpler and more efficient
children.curiosity: Schulman et al. (Berkeley) published TRPO in 2015. The paper established the theoretical foundation that motivated PPO — Schulman said that PPO was created because 'TRPO is difficult to implement correctly'.

children.name: TD3 (Twin Delayed DDPG)
children.diff_siblings: Improvement of DDPG with two critics (Twin) and delayed updates (Delayed) — different from DDPG for solving Q-value overestimation via min of the two critics
strengths: More stable than DDPG in continuous environments
weaknesses: More parameters than SAC (two critics + actor)
Slightly inferior performance to SAC in many environments
recommended_for: Robotics with continuous actions as an alternative to SAC
When SAC is hard to tune due to entropy maximization
not_recommended_for: SAC tends to outperform TD3 in most robotics benchmarks
children.curiosity: Fujimoto, Herke van Hoof, and Meger (McGill) published TD3 in 2018. The name captures the two innovations: Twin critics avoid overestimation; Delayed updates of the actor avoid error propagation.

children.name: Rainbow DQN
children.diff_siblings: Combination of 6 improvements over DQN: Double DQN, Prioritized Replay, Dueling Network, Multi-step, Distributional RL, and Noisy Nets — different from DQN for integrating all the best modifications
strengths: Combines all the best extensions of DQN
State of the art on Atari when published
Reference base for comparison of RL algorithms
weaknesses: Much more complex to implement than DQN
Individual benefits of each component are hard to separate
Replaced by more modern agents in complex environments
recommended_for: Benchmark and reference in RL research
not_recommended_for: Continuous environments — SAC or TD3
When implementation simplicity is a priority
children.curiosity: Hessel et al. (DeepMind) published Rainbow in 2017. The paper demonstrated that each of the 6 extensions contributes positively — but in different doses. Rainbow had better performance on Atari than any individual component.

children.name: HER (Hindsight Experience Replay)
children.diff_siblings: Replay technique that turns failed goals into success in different goals — solves exploration in environments with sparse reward without modifying the base algorithm
strengths: Solves sparse reward elegantly without reward shaping
Works with any off-policy algorithm (DDPG, SAC, TD3)
Learns from failures by reinterpreting them as success in another goal
weaknesses: Only for environments with defined goals (goal-conditioned)
recommended_for: Robotics with physical goals (reach position, push object)
Environments with sparse reward but well-defined goals
not_recommended_for: Environments without explicit goal structure
children.curiosity: Andrychowicz et al. (OpenAI) published HER in 2017. The intuition: 'even if we didn't reach the original goal, we learned something — where we ended up is a valid goal'. The idea transformed robotics with sparse reward.

children.name: IMPALA (Importance Weighted Actor-Learner Architecture)
children.diff_siblings: Scalable asynchronous RL with V-trace for off-policy correction — different from A3C by completely separating actors and learner; scales to hundreds of actors in parallel
strengths: Scales to hundreds of CPUs in parallel
weaknesses: More complex to implement than PPO
V-trace introduces bias vs exact IMPALA
Less popular in environments with limited hardware
recommended_for: Large-scale RL training with CPU clusters
When experience throughput is the bottleneck
not_recommended_for: Small environments — PPO or SAC are sufficient
children.curiosity: Espeholt et al. (DeepMind) published IMPALA in 2018. The clear separation between actors and learner allowed scaling RL to very complex environments — the basis of DeepMind's large-scale RL infrastructure.

children.name: Model-Based
children.diff_siblings: Learns an environment model and uses it for planning — more data-efficient; different from Model-Free by requiring a correct model
weaknesses: Model errors propagate to the policy
recommended_for: Physical environments where interactions are expensive
not_recommended_for: Very complex environments where an accurate model is infeasible
children.curiosity: AlphaZero (2017): with a perfect game model, uses MCTS for deep planning. In 4 hours, it surpassed decades of specialized chess programming.

children.name: Dyna-Q
children.diff_siblings: Integrates Q-Learning with a learned model — uses the model to generate simulated experiences; different from pure Q-Learning by using a model; different from pure Model-Based by learning the model iteratively
strengths: Combines Model-Based efficiency with Model-Free robustness
Planning with a model improves the Q-function
not_recommended_for: Very complex environments where an accurate model is infeasible
children.curiosity: Sutton proposed Dyna-Q in 1990. The insight: each real interaction can generate multiple 'simulated' interactions via the model — multiplying learning efficiency.

children.name: World Models
children.diff_siblings: Learns a generative environment model (VAE + MDN-RNN) and trains a controller in the imagined model — agent lives and learns in a 'dream'
strengths: Training in the imagined world — minimal real interactions
weaknesses: Complexity of training VAE + MDN-RNN jointly
recommended_for: Physical environments where exploration is expensive or dangerous
not_recommended_for: Environments where an accurate model is impossible
children.curiosity: Ha and Schmidhuber published 'World Models' in 2018. The title evokes philosophy: animals have an 'internal world model' to plan. The agent practices in the dream, like athletes who train mentally.

children.name: Multi-Agent
children.diff_siblings: Multiple agents interacting in a shared environment — different from single-agent RL by having a non-stationary environment (other agents also learn)
weaknesses: Coordination vs. competition requires careful design
not_recommended_for: Problem with a single decision-maker — single-agent RL
children.curiosity: Vinyals et al. (DeepMind) published AlphaStar in 2019 — surpassed human champions in StarCraft II, requiring coordination of multiple units in real time.

children.name: MADDPG
children.diff_siblings: Multi-Agent DDPG with centralized critic — different from independent DDPG because it trains the critic with observations from all agents; decentralized execution
strengths: Cooperation and competition in the same architecture
weaknesses: Critic grows with the number of agents
recommended_for: Cooperative and competitive games with a fixed number of agents
not_recommended_for: Many agents — MAPPO
children.curiosity: Lowe et al. (OpenAI) proposed MADDPG in 2017. The 'centralised training with decentralised execution' trick became the dominant paradigm in cooperative MARL.

children.name: QMIX
children.diff_siblings: Q-function factorization for cooperative agents — ensures consistency between individual Q and global Q via mixing network; standard in cooperative benchmarks
weaknesses: Mixing network is a black box
not_recommended_for: Competitive environments — MADDPG
children.curiosity: Rashid et al. (Oxford) proposed QMIX in 2018. The SMAC (StarCraft Multi-Agent Challenge) benchmark was developed by the same authors.

children.name: MAPPO (Multi-Agent PPO)
children.diff_siblings: Centralized PPO for multiple agents — different from MADDPG because it is on-policy and more stable; uses centralized critic during training and decentralized actors during execution
strengths: More stable than MADDPG during training
Simple to implement (direct extension of PPO)
Works well in cooperative environments with many agents
weaknesses: On-policy — less data efficient than MADDPG
Performance can be inferior to QMIX in specific cooperative benchmarks
recommended_for: When training stability outweighs data efficiency
not_recommended_for: Competitive environments — MADDPG or League of Agents
When data efficiency is critical
children.curiosity: Yu et al. published MAPPO in 2021. The surprising result: simple PPO with centralized critic competed with or outperformed much more complex MARL algorithms — the 'secret recipe' was the use of global Features in the critic.

children.name: 1.5 Causal / Heterogeneous Inference
children.diff_siblings: Estimates causal effects of interventions — differs from statistical correlation by answering 'what if?'; from prediction by focusing on causality
strengths: Estimates effects that pure observation cannot answer
weaknesses: Harder to implement than predictive models
recommended_for: A/B testing, public policy evaluation, medical treatment analysis
not_recommended_for: Pure prediction without causal question
children.curiosity: Judea Pearl developed the do-calculus in 1995, providing a mathematical foundation for causality. Pearl received the Turing Award in 2011.

children.name: Causal Forest
children.diff_siblings: Estimates Heterogeneous Treatment Effects via Random Forest — different from regression because it estimates individual effects; based on honest inference
strengths: Estimates heterogeneous effects for each individual
not_recommended_for: When average effect is sufficient — ATE with simple methods
children.curiosity: Wager and Athey published Causal Forest in 2018. The 'honest trees' innovation uses half the data to build the tree and the other half to estimate values — necessary for valid inference.

children.name: Double ML (DML)
children.diff_siblings: Uses ML to control confounders via partialling-out — different from Frisch-Waugh regression because it uses ML instead of linear; theoretically grounded via semiparametrics
strengths: Uses any ML model to control confounders
recommended_for: When confounders are many and the relationship is complex
not_recommended_for: Experimental data — randomization solves confounding
children.curiosity: Chernozhukov et al. published DML in 2018. The insight: ML regularization introduces bias in causal estimates — cross-fitting removes this bias.

children.name: Synthetic Control
children.diff_siblings: Creates a synthetic control unit as a weighted combination of similar units — different from DiD because it does not require a pre-existing control group
strengths: Does not require a pre-existing control group
weaknesses: Works only with 1 or few treated
recommended_for: Evaluation of regional or national policies
not_recommended_for: Many treated — DiD
children.curiosity: Abadie, Diamond, and Hainmueller published in 2010. The original example was the effect of California's anti-smoking program — the synthetic California was built by weighting other states.

children.name: PSM (Propensity Score Matching)
children.diff_siblings: Matches treated and controls by estimated treatment probability — creates comparable groups like a quasi-experiment
weaknesses: Discards data outside the overlap region
recommended_for: Observational studies in epidemiology and health
not_recommended_for: When unobserved confounders are suspected — IV
children.curiosity: Rosenbaum and Rubin proposed PSM in 1983. The key result: conditioning only on the propensity score (scalar) is sufficient to balance all observed covariates.

children.name: IPW (Inverse Probability Weighting)
children.diff_siblings: Reweighs observations by the inverse of the treatment probability — different from PSM because it does not discard data; basis of TMLE
strengths: Horvitz-Thompson estimator with clean theoretical properties
weaknesses: Highly sensitive to extreme propensity scores
Less efficient than doubly robust estimators
recommended_for: As a component of TMLE or AIPW
not_recommended_for: When propensity scores are extreme
children.curiosity: Horvitz and Thompson developed IPW in 1952 for complex sampling. Observations with low probability of receiving treatment are 'rare' and must be upweighted.

children.name: TMLE (Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation)
children.diff_siblings: Doubly robust estimator — consistent if outcome OR propensity model is correct; combines outcome model and propensity score
recommended_for: When maximum efficiency and robustness are needed
not_recommended_for: Simple analyses where PSM or DML are sufficient
children.curiosity: Van der Laan and Rubin proposed TMLE in 2006 combining semiparametric theory with ML.

children.name: DiD (Differences-in-Differences)
children.diff_siblings: Compares change in treated group vs. control before and after treatment — assumes parallel trends; controls for time-invariant confounders
recommended_for: Policy evaluation with natural control group
not_recommended_for: When parallel trends are implausible
children.curiosity: Some attribute the origin of DiD to John Snow in 1855 — analysis of the cholera epidemic in London — a DiD analysis avant la lettre 170 years before the name existed.

children.name: IV / 2SLS (Instrumental Variables)
children.diff_siblings: Uses instrument correlated with treatment but not with error — corrects endogeneity; estimates local effect (LATE)
strengths: Estimates causal effect with unobserved confounders
weaknesses: Weak instrument leads to very noisy estimates
not_recommended_for: When valid instrument does not exist — DML
children.curiosity: Wright proposed IV in 1928. The 2021 Nobel Prize in Economics (Card, Angrist, Imbens) was partly for development and application of IV.

children.name: Regression Discontinuity (RD)
children.diff_siblings: Explores discontinuity in treatment probability around a threshold to identify causal effect — different from DiD in not requiring a control group; from IV in not requiring an instrument
strengths: Robust local identification around the threshold
Intuitive design — compares units just below and above the cutoff
weaknesses: Estimated effect is local to the threshold — limited external validity
Requires sharp discontinuity — score manipulation invalidates
Requires many observations close to the threshold for precision
recommended_for: When there is a threshold or cutoff in eligibility criteria
Evaluation of programs with cutoff criteria (minimum income, cutoff score, risk index)
not_recommended_for: When there is no natural threshold in the data — DiD or IV
children.curiosity: Thistlethwaite and Campbell proposed RD in 1960. The design uses the discontinuity as an exogenous source of variation — units just below the threshold are the perfect control group for units just above.

children.name: Front-Door Criterion (Causal Mediation)
children.diff_siblings: Identifies causal effect via mediator variable when unobserved confounders exist — different from IV in not needing an external instrument; uses causal DAG structure
strengths: Identifies causal effect without external instrument
Uses natural mediators as identification path
Theoretical basis in Judea Pearl's do-calculus
weaknesses: Requires mediator satisfying specific DAG conditions
Rarely applicable in practice — valid mediators are hard to find
More abstract than IV or DiD for practical implementation
recommended_for: When natural mediator exists and IV is not available
Causal analysis with known DAG structure
not_recommended_for: When IV or DiD are available and simpler
When mediator does not satisfy front-door conditions
children.curiosity: Judea Pearl proposed the Front-Door Criterion in 1995 as part of the do-calculus. The classic example: estimating the effect of smoking on cancer via tar in the lungs as a mediator — without needing to control for all confounders.

children.name: 1.6 Transfer Learning (Classic ML)
children.diff_siblings: Transfers knowledge from source task to target task with few data — different from DL Fine-tuning by operating on classic features and models
strengths: Reduces need for labeled data in target task
weaknesses: Negative transfer can worsen the target model
recommended_for: Domain adaptation in NLP and vision with limited data
not_recommended_for: Very different domains — negative transfer
children.curiosity: Pan and Yang published the survey 'A Survey on Transfer Learning' in 2010. The concept: not learning from scratch — analogous to human learning.

children.name: Domain Adaptation
children.diff_siblings: Adapts a source domain model to a target domain with a different distribution — differs from Transfer Learning by focusing on distribution change (covariate shift)
strengths: Handles covariate shift without labels in the target
recommended_for: NLP: adapting a model from tweets to scientific articles
not_recommended_for: Completely different domains with no clear relationship
children.curiosity: Blitzer et al. proposed Structural Correspondence Learning in 2006. The problem motivated research that culminated in pre-trained language models like BERT.

children.name: Multi-Task Learning (Classic ML)
children.diff_siblings: Trains simultaneously on multiple related tasks — differs from Transfer Learning by learning all tasks simultaneously; improves generalization via indirect regularization
not_recommended_for: Tasks with conflicting objectives
children.curiosity: Rich Caruana proposed Multi-Task Learning in 1997. Learning a related task acts as a regularizer — forces the model to learn features that generalize.

children.name: 2. AI / Deep Learning
children.diff_siblings: Deep Learning uses deep neural networks for automatic hierarchical representations — differs from classic ML by scaling with data and computation; from Statistics by not having explicit parametric assumptions; requires GPU and large volumes of data
strengths: State of the art in image, text, audio, and video
weaknesses: Requires GPU and large volumes of data
recommended_for: Images, text, audio, video, and high-dimensional data
not_recommended_for: Small datasets — classic ML often outperforms
When interpretability is a regulatory requirement
children.curiosity: McCulloch and Pitts proposed the first artificial neuron in 1943. The field went through two 'AI winters' before the renaissance with AlexNet in 2012.

children.name: 2.1 Classic Networks
children.diff_siblings: Basic architectures without convolutions or recurrence — differ from CNN by not having translational invariance; from RNN by not processing sequences; foundation of all neural networks
weaknesses: Scale poorly with high dimension without CNNs
not_recommended_for: Images — CNN
Text — RNN/Transformer
children.curiosity: The MLP was the first network capable of learning XOR — the problem Minsky/Papert used to 'kill' the Perceptron in 1969. The solution arrived with backpropagation in 1986.

children.name: MLP (Multilayer Perceptron)
children.diff_siblings: Dense network with hidden layers and backpropagation — universal approximator; differs from CNNs and RNNs by not having a specific structure
weaknesses: Does not exploit spatial or temporal structure
recommended_for: Tabular data with complex non-linear relationships
not_recommended_for: Images — CNN
Sequences — RNN/Transformer
children.curiosity: Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams published backpropagation in 1986 in Nature — one of the most cited papers in computer science.

children.name: RBF Network (Radial Basis Function)
children.diff_siblings: Hidden layer with Gaussian functions centered on prototypes — local activations instead of global; different from MLP for having local receptive field
weaknesses: Number of centers is a critical hyperparameter
not_recommended_for: High dimensionality
Modern applications — MLP with dropout
children.curiosity: Broomhead and Lowe proposed RBF Networks in 1988. With the revival of DL via GPUs in the 2010s, they were largely forgotten.

children.name: ELM (Extreme Learning Machine)
children.diff_siblings: Hidden layer weights are random and fixed — only output weights are trained via pseudo-inverse; 1-step training, extremely fast
not_recommended_for: Maximum performance — MLP with Adam outperforms
children.curiosity: Huang et al. proposed ELM in 2006. The method generated controversy — critics argued that random weights were wasteful of capacity.

children.name: 2.2 Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN)
children.diff_siblings: Apply local convolutional filters — translational invariance via shared weights; differ from MLP for efficiency on spatial data; from ViT for local processing
weaknesses: Inferior performance to ViT on very large datasets
not_recommended_for: Text and long sequences — Transformer
children.curiosity: LeCun et al. published LeNet in 1989. CNNs remained dormant until AlexNet (2012) which reduced the error on ImageNet by 10pp — starting the modern era of Deep Learning.

children.name: LeNet
children.diff_siblings: First successful CNN — uses tanh/sigmoid; smaller than modern networks; deployed at USPS for reading ZIP codes
not_recommended_for: Any practical application — ResNet is superior
children.curiosity: LeCun et al. published LeNet in 1998. The system processed 10% of all checks in the USA in the 1990s — the first large-scale production application of DL.

children.name: AlexNet
children.diff_siblings: Winner of ImageNet 2012 — introduced ReLU, dropout and training on multiple GPUs; started the modern era of Deep Learning
weaknesses: Much less efficient than modern ResNet
not_recommended_for: Any practical application — ResNet50 is more accurate
children.curiosity: Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton reduced the top-5 error on ImageNet from 26% to 15%. It was the moment the community realized deep learning would dominate computer vision.

children.name: VGG
children.diff_siblings: Deep architecture with stacked 3×3 filters — showed that depth matters; without skip connections like ResNet
recommended_for: Transfer learning when ResNet is not available
not_recommended_for: Modern applications — ResNet or EfficientNet
children.curiosity: Simonyan and Zisserman (Oxford) published VGG in 2014. Stacking multiple 3×3 convolutions became standard. VGG16 weights are still widely used in transfer learning.

children.name: ResNet
children.diff_siblings: Residual connections (skip connections) that allow networks of hundreds of layers — differs from VGG by solving vanishing gradient with shortcuts
strengths: Solves vanishing gradient in deep networks
weaknesses: ViT outperforms on very large datasets
not_recommended_for: High-resolution images — ViT
Lightweight — EfficientNet
children.curiosity: He, Zhang, Ren and Sun (Microsoft) published ResNet in 2015 with an error of 3.57% on ImageNet — better than humans (5.1%). The skip connections were inspired by LSTM.

children.name: EfficientNet
children.diff_siblings: Scales width, depth, and resolution via compound scaling — better accuracy-per-FLOP trade-off
weaknesses: Replaced by ViT on very large datasets
not_recommended_for: Maximum performance — ViT-L with abundant data
children.curiosity: Tan and Le (Google Brain) published EfficientNet in 2019. EfficientNet-B7 achieved 84.3% on ImageNet with 66M parameters — while GPipe used 557M for the same result.

children.name: YOLO (You Only Look Once)
children.diff_siblings: Real-time object detection as regression — processes the entire image in one pass; growing family (v1-v10+)
strengths: One pass through the network — very efficient
not_recommended_for: Maximum accuracy — DETR
children.curiosity: Redmon et al. published YOLO in 2016. Joseph Redmon retired from research in 2020 citing ethical concerns regarding military use.

children.name: GoogLeNet / Inception
children.diff_siblings: Inception modules process multiple filter sizes in parallel — different from VGG for being more computationally efficient; from ResNet for using width instead of skip connections
weaknesses: More complex to implement than VGG
not_recommended_for: Detection — ResNet has a better backbone
children.curiosity: Szegedy et al. (Google) published GoogLeNet in 2014. The name is a tribute to LeCun's LeNet. InceptionV3 (2016) and InceptionV4 are still used in production for their efficiency.

children.name: DenseNet (Densely Connected CNN)
children.diff_siblings: Each layer receives features from ALL previous layers — different from ResNet because it has dense connections (not just a single-layer skip); reuses features maximally
strengths: Fewer parameters than ResNet for the same performance
Gradients flow directly to any layer
weaknesses: Very high memory usage during training
recommended_for: When parameter efficiency is a priority
not_recommended_for: Very large datasets — ResNet is more scalable
children.curiosity: Huang et al. published DenseNet in 2017. The phrase 'dense connections' captures: each layer concatenates the feature maps from all previous layers — resulting in increasingly larger input tensors.

children.name: MobileNet
children.diff_siblings: Depth-wise and point-wise separable convolutions — different from standard CNNs because it reduces operations by 8-9× with little loss of accuracy; designed for mobile and IoT
strengths: Much faster and lighter than standard CNNs
MobileNetV3 is still competitive in efficiency benchmarks
Designed for deployment on resource-constrained devices
weaknesses: Inferior performance to ResNet/EfficientNet in high accuracy
Less suitable for fine-grained detection tasks
recommended_for: Inference on mobile, embedded, and IoT devices
When inference latency is a critical constraint
not_recommended_for: Maximum performance without hardware constraints
children.curiosity: Howard et al. (Google) published MobileNet in 2017. The depthwise separable convolution was invented by Sifre in 2014 for SigNet — MobileNet popularized it.

children.name: U-Net
children.diff_siblings: Encoder-decoder architecture with skip connections for medical image segmentation — different from classification CNNs because it produces a pixel-to-pixel segmentation map; different from DETR because it is convolutional
strengths: Excellent segmentation performance with few data
Skip connections between encoder and decoder preserve spatial details
weaknesses: Designed for medical data — less effective on natural images
Replaced by Swin/Mask2Former in natural benchmarks
recommended_for: Medical image segmentation: tumors, organs, cells
Segmentation of scientific data with few examples
not_recommended_for: Natural image segmentation in general benchmarks — Mask2Former
children.curiosity: Ronneberger, Fischer and Brox published U-Net in 2015 for segmenting neurons in electron microscopes. With only 30 training images, U-Net outperformed previous methods. Today it is the standard backbone in radiology AI.

children.name: 2.3 Recurrent Neural Networks (RNN)
children.diff_siblings: Maintain internal state between steps — process variable-length sequences; differ from CNNs by processing sequentially; from Transformers by not processing in parallel
weaknesses: Largely surpassed by Transformers in NLP
not_recommended_for: Modern NLP — Transformers are superior
children.curiosity: LSTM (1997) solved the vanishing gradient and dominated NLP until 2018, when Transformers took over.

children.name: RNN Vanilla (Elman)
children.diff_siblings: Hidden state propagated by sigmoid — simplest possible; vanishing gradient prevents learning dependencies beyond ~10 steps
not_recommended_for: Any practical application
children.curiosity: Hochreiter (1991) identified the vanishing gradient in his dissertation. In 1997, he proposed LSTM as a solution.

children.name: LSTM
children.diff_siblings: Input, forget, and output gates control flow — solves vanishing gradient; differs from GRU by having 3 gates instead of 2
not_recommended_for: Modern NLP — BERT/GPT are superior
children.curiosity: Hochreiter and Schmidhuber published LSTM in 1997. The iPhone uses LSTM for predictive keyboard — one of the first applications on billions of devices.

children.name: GRU
children.diff_siblings: 2 gates (reset and update) — simpler and faster than LSTM; similar performance in most tasks
weaknesses: Slightly inferior to LSTM in long dependencies
recommended_for: When LSTM is too slow for the hardware
not_recommended_for: Modern NLP — Transformers are superior
children.curiosity: Cho et al. proposed GRU in 2014. The same paper introduced the encoder-decoder architecture that revolutionized NLP.

children.name: Bidirectional RNN/LSTM
children.diff_siblings: Processes sequence in both directions — incorporates future context; different from unidirectional RNN; basis of pre-BERT (ELMo)
recommended_for: NLP where full context is available
not_recommended_for: Text generation — future context unavailable
children.curiosity: Schuster and Paliwal proposed BiRNN in 1997. ELMo (2018) used deep BiLSTM — the direct precursor to BERT.

children.name: Encoder-Decoder (Seq2Seq)
children.diff_siblings: Architecture that compresses input sequence into context vector via LSTM encoder and decodes via LSTM decoder — basis of machine translation and sequence generation
strengths: Maps variable-length sequences to variable sequences
weaknesses: Fixed context vector bottleneck — attention solves
Slow training due to sequential nature
not_recommended_for: Modern NLP — Transformers (T5, BART) completely outperform
children.curiosity: Sutskever, Vinyals, and Le (Google) published Seq2Seq in 2014. The encoder-decoder architecture became the dominant paradigm in NLP for 4 years — until being replaced by Transformers in 2018.

children.name: Attention Mechanism (Bahdanau)
children.diff_siblings: Attention mechanism that allows the decoder to focus on relevant parts of the encoder instead of using a fixed vector — direct precursor to Transformer; different from Luong attention for being additive
strengths: Solves the fixed context vector bottleneck
More interpretable — attention map shows alignment
Substantial improvement in long sequence translation
recommended_for: Sequences where interpretable alignment is needed
not_recommended_for: Modern NLP — Transformers have much more efficient attention
children.curiosity: Bahdanau, Cho, and Bengio published the attention mechanism in 2015 for machine translation. It is the paper that directly inspired the Transformer's multi-head attention in 2017 — Vaswani et al. explicitly cite it.

children.name: 2.4 Transformers
children.diff_siblings: Multi-head attention mechanism that processes all tokens in parallel — different from RNNs for being parallelizable; from CNNs for having global receptive field; scalable with data and parameters
strengths: Parallel attention — trains much faster than RNNs
weaknesses: Attention is O(n²) in sequence length
Requires much more data than RNNs to surpass
recommended_for: NLP, vision, multimodal, time series — universal architecture
not_recommended_for: Very long sequences without modifications — SSMs are more efficient
children.curiosity: Vaswani et al. (Google) published 'Attention is All You Need' in 2017. With over 80,000 citations, it is one of the most influential in ML history.

children.name: Transformers NLP
children.diff_siblings: For natural language processing — encoder vs. decoder vs. encoder-decoder defines tasks; pre-trained models transferable to any NLP task
weaknesses: Bias and toxicity in training data
recommended_for: Any NLP task: classification, generation, translation, Q&A
not_recommended_for: Very limited hardware — DistilBERT or FastText
children.curiosity: BERT (2018) and GPT-3 (2020) transformed NLP irreversibly.

children.name: BERT
children.diff_siblings: Pre-trained bidirectional encoder with Masked LM and NSP — different from GPT for being an encoder (not generation); from RoBERTa for using less data
weaknesses: Pure encoder — does not generate text
not_recommended_for: Text generation — GPT
Long sequences — Longformer
children.curiosity: Devlin et al. (Google) published BERT in 2018. The paradigm: pre-train on massive text, fine-tune with few examples.

children.name: GPT / GPT-4
children.diff_siblings: Pre-trained autoregressive decoder for generation — unidirectional; GPT-3/4 exhibit emergence with scale; base of ChatGPT
not_recommended_for: Comprehension tasks — BERT is more efficient
children.curiosity: Brown et al. published GPT-3 in 2020. The discovery of few-shot learning without fine-tuning was the biggest surprise.

children.name: RoBERTa
children.diff_siblings: BERT with optimized training — more data (10×), no NSP, larger batches; shows that BERT was undertrained
not_recommended_for: Text generation — decoder models
children.curiosity: Liu et al. (Facebook AI) published RoBERTa in 2019. With no new architecture, just careful engineering, it surpassed BERT in everything.

children.name: T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer)
children.diff_siblings: Frames all NLP tasks as text-to-text — encoder-decoder; different from BERT (encoder-only) and GPT (decoder-only)
weaknesses: More parameters than BERT for the same understanding
not_recommended_for: Pure text generation — GPT-style
children.curiosity: Raffel et al. (Google) published T5 in 2019 along with the C4 dataset.

children.name: Longformer
children.diff_siblings: Local + global sparse attention — reduces complexity from O(n²) to O(n); for documents up to 4096 tokens
weaknesses: Performance slightly inferior to BERT on short sentences
not_recommended_for: Very long sequences (>4096) — BigBird or Mamba
children.curiosity: Beltagy et al. (AI2) published Longformer in 2020. First to make BERT practical for long documents via sliding window attention.

children.name: BigBird
children.diff_siblings: Sparse attention with random, local, and global components — more powerful than Longformer; theoretically Turing-complete
not_recommended_for: Sequences above 16k tokens — Mamba
children.curiosity: Zaheer et al. (Google) published BigBird in 2020. Applications in genomics were the motivating use case.

children.name: Sparse Transformer
children.diff_siblings: Strided sparse attention — reduces from O(n²) to O(n√n); proposed for pixel-by-pixel image generation
not_recommended_for: General NLP — Longformer is simpler
children.curiosity: Child et al. (OpenAI) published Sparse Transformer in 2019. Anticipated the explosion of image generation via DL.

children.name: XLNet
children.diff_siblings: Permutation autoregressive model — captures bidirectional context like BERT but without masking; different from BERT by modeling dependencies of all tokens via permutation
strengths: Better than BERT on some NLP benchmarks
Generalizes BERT and GPT in a single framework
weaknesses: Much slower to train than BERT
Benefits over BERT are inconsistent across tasks
Replaced by larger models like DeBERTa
recommended_for: NLP tasks where BERT's mask bias is problematic
not_recommended_for: Most applications — BERT or RoBERTa are faster and sufficient
children.curiosity: Yang et al. (CMU and Google Brain) published XLNet in 2019. The argument: BERT assumes masked tokens are independent of each other — XLNet fixes this limitation via training permutations.

children.name: ALBERT
children.diff_siblings: BERT with parameter sharing and embedding factorization — 18× fewer parameters than BERT-large with similar performance; different from DistilBERT for not using knowledge distillation
weaknesses: Slower than BERT in inference (despite fewer parameters)
Similar but not superior performance to BERT
recommended_for: When memory is a constraint but BERT performance is needed
not_recommended_for: When inference speed is a priority — DistilBERT
When maximum performance is needed — DeBERTa
children.curiosity: Lan et al. (Google Research and TTIC) published ALBERT in 2019. The counterintuitive insight: sharing parameters between layers does not degrade performance — and acts as regularization.

children.name: DistilBERT
children.diff_siblings: BERT compressed via knowledge distillation — 40% smaller, 60% faster, retains 97% of performance; different from ALBERT for using distillation instead of parameter sharing
strengths: Performance close to BERT on downstream tasks
