weaknesses: Distillation requires training the teacher (BERT) first
recommended_for: Deploy on devices with memory and latency constraints
Production applications where BERT is too slow
not_recommended_for: Maximum performance — BERT or DeBERTa
Research where a full benchmark is needed
children.curiosity: Sanh et al. (Hugging Face) published DistilBERT in 2019. The success democratized the use of BERT — made BERT-quality models accessible on smartphones and edge devices.

children.name: DeBERTa
children.diff_siblings: BERT with disentangled attention (content and position separated) — outperforms BERT and RoBERTa on SuperGLUE; different for modeling relative position separately from content
strengths: Outperforms BERT and RoBERTa on SuperGLUE benchmarks
Better captures positional relations between tokens
weaknesses: More complex to implement and tune
recommended_for: When maximum performance on NLP understanding tasks is needed
not_recommended_for: Text generation — GPT-style
Applications with latency constraints
children.curiosity: He et al. (Microsoft) published DeBERTa in 2021. DeBERTa v3 combines disentangled attention with ELECTRA's replaced token detection — outperforming BERT-large with fewer parameters.

children.name: LLaMA / Mistral
children.diff_siblings: High-efficiency open-weight language models — different from GPT-4 for being open-source; from BERT for being decoder-only for generation; Mistral uses sliding window attention
strengths: Base for the explosion of open-source models (Llama2, Llama3)
weaknesses: Requires GPU with 16-80GB VRAM for full inference
No technical support like proprietary models
recommended_for: Local fine-tuning of LLMs without API dependency
Applications where data privacy prevents use of external services
not_recommended_for: State-of-the-art performance — GPT-4 or Claude
children.curiosity: Meta AI published LLaMA in 2023. Mistral AI published Mistral 7B in 2023 — outperforming LLaMA 2 13B with half the parameters. These models triggered an explosion of open-source models.

children.name: ELECTRA
children.diff_siblings: Trains via replaced token detection instead of masking — different from BERT for using a discriminator (not masked LM); much more efficient: uses ALL tokens in training, not just 15%
strengths: 15× more efficient in training than BERT
Uses 100% of tokens for learning (vs 15% of BERT)
Superior performance to BERT with same training resources
weaknesses: Less popular than BERT/RoBERTa despite being more efficient
recommended_for: Training BERT-quality models with lower computational budget
not_recommended_for: When pre-training is not the goal — fine-tuning an already available BERT
children.curiosity: Clark et al. (Google Brain) published ELECTRA in 2020. The insight: learning to distinguish real tokens from generated tokens is much more efficient than learning to predict masked tokens — uses the full context at every step.

children.name: Vision Transformers
children.diff_siblings: Transformers applied to images via patchification — differ from CNNs by having a global receptive field; more powerful with sufficient training data
strengths: Global attention captures long-range spatial dependencies
Better performance than CNNs with very large datasets
weaknesses: Inferior to CNNs with small datasets (<1M images)
recommended_for: Classification and segmentation with large datasets
not_recommended_for: Small datasets — CNNs like EfficientNet
children.curiosity: ViT (2020) showed that pure Transformers outperform CNNs in vision when pre-trained on sufficient data.

children.name: ViT (Vision Transformer)
children.diff_siblings: Divides image into 16×16 patches and applies Transformer — without convolutions; different from Swin in not having a hierarchy
strengths: Global attention from the first layer
weaknesses: Inferior to CNNs with less than ~14M images
not_recommended_for: Small datasets — EfficientNet
children.curiosity: Dosovitskiy et al. (Google) published ViT in 2020: 'An Image is Worth 16×16 Words'.

children.name: Swin Transformer
children.diff_siblings: ViT with patch hierarchy and window-based attention — different from ViT by having multiple scales; state-of-the-art in detection and segmentation
strengths: Window-based attention — efficient for high resolution
recommended_for: Backbone for object detection and segmentation
not_recommended_for: Simple classification — ViT with massive pre-training
children.curiosity: Liu et al. (Microsoft) published Swin in 2021. The insight: bring the hierarchy of CNNs to Transformers.

children.name: DETR
children.diff_siblings: End-to-end object detection via Transformer — without NMS and without anchor boxes
weaknesses: Much slower to train than YOLO
not_recommended_for: Real-time — YOLO is much faster
children.curiosity: Carion et al. (Facebook AI) published DETR in 2020. The removal of NMS — a ubiquitous non-differentiable component — was the main breakthrough.

children.name: Multimodal Transformers
children.diff_siblings: Combine text, image, and other modalities — differ from single-modal models by learning cross-modal alignment; basis for text-to-image generation
weaknesses: Require huge volumes of paired data
not_recommended_for: Single-modal tasks where specialized models outperform
children.curiosity: CLIP (2021) demonstrated that text-image alignment enables zero-shot classification without seeing a single example.

children.name: CLIP
children.diff_siblings: Aligns text and image via contrastive learning on 400M pairs — zero-shot classification; different from DALL-E for being only an encoder (no generation)
strengths: Base of DALL-E, Stable Diffusion, and LLaVA
not_recommended_for: Image generation — Stable Diffusion
children.curiosity: Radford et al. (OpenAI) published CLIP in 2021. Zero-shot on ImageNet (76.2%) was comparable to ResNet-50 trained on full ImageNet.

children.name: LLaVA
children.diff_siblings: Connects vision encoder (CLIP) with LLM via projection layer — allows multimodal chat with images; different from CLIP for generating text
strengths: Visual instruction tuning with few data
recommended_for: Multimodal chat with images in open-source systems
not_recommended_for: Maximum multimodal performance — GPT-4V
children.curiosity: Liu et al. (UW-Madison) published LLaVA in 2023. Used GPT-4 to generate synthetic visual instruction data — creating a high-quality dataset without expensive human annotation.

children.name: DALL-E / DALL-E 3
children.diff_siblings: Text-to-image generation via discrete tokens (VQ-VAE) + Transformer or via Diffusion (v3) — different from CLIP for generating images; from Stable Diffusion for being proprietary and focused on following precise instructions
strengths: Excellent at following complex textual instructions
DALL-E 3 integrated into ChatGPT for conversational generation
recommended_for: High-quality image generation following complex instructions
not_recommended_for: Open-source and customization — Stable Diffusion
When full model control is needed
children.curiosity: Ramesh et al. (OpenAI) published DALL-E in 2021. DALL-E 3 (2023) was co-developed with Anthropic to reduce instruction errors — uses CLIP to improve text-image alignment during the generation process.

children.name: Flamingo
children.diff_siblings: Visual language model that processes interleaved images and text — different from LLaVA for being created from scratch (does not combine CLIP + LLM); visual few-shot learning
strengths: Visual few-shot learning — solves tasks with only 4-32 examples
Naturally processes text interleaved with images
Foundation of GPT-4V and modern multimodal models
weaknesses: Requires massive pre-training on text-image pairs
not_recommended_for: Practical applications — LLaVA or GPT-4V are more accessible
children.curiosity: Alayrac et al. (DeepMind) published Flamingo in 2022. The model was trained on 43 billion image-text pairs from the web. Flamingo was the proof of concept that LLMs can be extended to multimodality with few architectural changes.

children.name: BLIP / BLIP-2
children.diff_siblings: Bootstrap Language-Image Pre-training — trains with noisy web data via bootstrapped filtering; different from CLIP for having generative capability; from LLaVA for training alignment explicitly
strengths: Noisy web data used efficiently via bootstrapping
BLIP-2 uses Q-Former for efficient alignment
weaknesses: Less popular than CLIP for embeddings
BLIP-2 still requires external LLM for generation
recommended_for: Image captioning and VQA (Visual Question Answering)
When text generation from images is needed
not_recommended_for: Image classification — CLIP is more efficient
Image generation — Diffusion or DALL-E
children.curiosity: Li et al. (Salesforce Research) published BLIP in 2022. The bootstrapping of noisy web data was inspired by semi-supervised learning techniques — creates high-quality training pairs from noisy data automatically.

children.name: Time Series Transformers
children.diff_siblings: Transformers for time series — differ from RNNs by processing in parallel; from NLP Transformers by having specific temporal encodings
not_recommended_for: Short series where ARIMA/ETS are sufficient
children.curiosity: TFT (2019) was the pioneer. The explosion of foundation models (Chronos, TimeGPT) in 2023-2024 followed the same pattern as NLP.

children.name: PatchTST
children.diff_siblings: Divides time series into patches (like ViT for images) — state-of-the-art performance on long-horizon benchmarks
strengths: Superior performance to LSTM and N-BEATS on long horizon
weaknesses: No series-specific mechanisms — can be suboptimal for seasonality
not_recommended_for: Short series — ARIMA
children.curiosity: Nie et al. published PatchTST in 2023. The insight was imported from ViT: splitting the series into patches reduces the attention cost.

children.name: iTransformer
children.diff_siblings: Inverts attention dimensions — applies attention between variables instead of between timesteps; state of the art in multivariate benchmarks
strengths: Attention between variables captures multivariate correlations
State of the art in multivariate benchmarks
recommended_for: Multivariate series with correlations between variables
not_recommended_for: Univariate series — the inversion does not help
children.curiosity: Liu et al. published iTransformer in 2024. The counterintuitive result — attention between variables, not timesteps — sparked debate about the real role of attention in time series.

children.name: DeepAR (Amazon)
children.diff_siblings: Probabilistic autoregressive model for time series — models full distribution via RNN; different from Prophet for being probabilistic and from point models for returning quantile intervals
strengths: Robust for series with short history using information from similar series
weaknesses: Requires many related series for effective training
More complex than ETS for single series
recommended_for: Demand forecasting at scale with uncertainty (Amazon, e-commerce)
Multiple related series where globalization helps
not_recommended_for: Single series with long history — ARIMA or ETS are sufficient
When prediction intervals are not needed
children.curiosity: Salinas et al. (Amazon Research) published DeepAR in 2019. Amazon uses DeepAR for demand forecasting of millions of products — the first foundation model for time series in large-scale industrial production.

children.name: TCN (Temporal Convolutional Network)
children.diff_siblings: CNN with dilated causal convolutions for time series — different from LSTM for being parallelizable; different from Transformer for using convolutions instead of attention; receptive field controlled by dilation
strengths: Parallelizable — much faster than LSTM for training
No vanishing gradient — gradients propagate directly
weaknesses: No capture of very long dependencies without many layers
Less flexible than Transformer for sequences with complex structure
Popularity decreased with the rise of Transformers
recommended_for: Time series forecasting as an efficient alternative to LSTM
When parallelism is more important than attention flexibility
not_recommended_for: Very long sequences — Mamba or SSM are more efficient
NLP — Transformers dominate
children.curiosity: Bai, Kolter and Koltun (CMU) published TCN in 2018 demonstrating that CNNs outperform LSTMs in time series benchmarks. The paper was received with skepticism — but influenced a whole generation of time series models.

children.name: Informer
children.diff_siblings: Transformer with ProbSparse attention for long horizons — different from standard Transformer by reducing complexity from O(n²) to O(n log n); focused on long-horizon forecasting
strengths: Reduces attention complexity from O(n²) to O(n log n)
weaknesses: ProbSparse attention may miss important dependencies
Performance questioned by subsequent papers (Is Transformer a bad predictor?)
Replaced by simpler approaches in recent benchmarks
not_recommended_for: Short horizons — simpler models outperform
children.curiosity: Zhou et al. published Informer at AAAI 2021 (Best Paper). Subsequent papers (Are Transformers Effective for Time Series Forecasting?, 2022) showed that simple linear models often outperform Informer — sparking debate about the real value of Transformers in time series.

children.name: Autoformer
children.diff_siblings: Transformer with series decomposition + auto-correlation — different from Transformer by replacing attention with auto-correlation in the frequency domain; explicitly decomposes trend and seasonality
strengths: Explicit decomposition of trend and seasonality
Better than Transformer for series with strong seasonality
weaknesses: Less effective in series without clear seasonality
Replaced by simpler models in many benchmarks
recommended_for: Series with strong seasonality and medium-long horizons
not_recommended_for: Series without seasonality — linear models or Prophet are simpler
children.curiosity: Wu et al. published Autoformer at NeurIPS 2021. Auto-correlation in the frequency domain is an alternative to attention that naturally captures periodic patterns — an elegant intuition for time series.

children.name: TimesNet
children.diff_siblings: Transforms 1D time series into 2D images and applies 2D CNN — different from Transformers by capturing intra-period and inter-period temporal variations via 2D structure; innovative approach
strengths: Captures both intra-period and inter-period variations
2D CNN is much more efficient than attention for repetitive patterns
State-of-the-art in multiple benchmarks (forecasting, imputation, anomaly detection)
weaknesses: 1D→2D transformation may lose information from aperiodic series
Period hyperparameter requires specification or estimation
recommended_for: Multitask time series: forecasting + imputation + anomaly detection
not_recommended_for: Series without clear periodicity
When interpretability of components is necessary
children.curiosity: Wu et al. published TimesNet at ICLR 2023. The insight of transforming 1D series into 2D representation was inspired by computer vision — each row of the image represents a period, each column an intra-period position.

children.name: 2.5 State Space Models (SSM)
children.diff_siblings: State space models with structured convolutions — train in parallel like Transformer but infer in O(1) like RNN; scale linearly O(n)
weaknesses: Performance in NLP slightly inferior to Transformers
not_recommended_for: Short sequences where Transformers are efficient
children.curiosity: Gu et al. published S4 in 2021. Mamba (2023) made the approach practical and competitive with Transformers.

children.name: S4 (Structured State Spaces)
children.diff_siblings: Parameterizes differential equations via HiPPO — end-to-end trainable; more efficient than Transformers on long sequences via FFT
weaknesses: Performance slightly inferior to Transformer in NLP
not_recommended_for: Standard NLP — Transformers have a mature ecosystem
children.curiosity: Gu, Goel and Ré published S4 in 2021. The motivation: 1-second audio files at 16kHz have 16,000 timesteps — too long for Transformers.

children.name: Mamba
children.diff_siblings: Selective SSM with selection mechanism — data-dependent (state transition depends on input); performance comparable to Transformer with linear scale
strengths: Data-dependent selection — much more expressive than S4
weaknesses: Still inferior to Transformer in mainstream NLP
recommended_for: Very long sequences: genomics, audio, video
not_recommended_for: Text with standard sequences where Transformers dominate
children.curiosity: Gu and Dao published Mamba in 2023. The selection mechanism — state space matrices depend on input — made SSMs competitive with Transformers.

children.name: Hyena / RetNet / RWKV
children.diff_siblings: Linear alternatives to Transformer — Hyena uses implicit convolution; RetNet adds retention; RWKV is linear recurrent; all with goal of O(n)
recommended_for: Research of efficient alternatives to Transformer
not_recommended_for: Production applications — Mamba or Transformer have more mature ecosystems
children.curiosity: Poli et al. (Hyena), Sun et al. (RetNet), and Peng et al. (RWKV) published in 2023. The race for O(n) alternatives to Transformer is one of the most active research fronts.

children.name: 2.6 Generative Models
children.diff_siblings: Learn the data distribution to generate new examples — differ from discriminative ones by modeling P(X) instead of P(Y|X); basis of all modern generative AI
recommended_for: Generation of images, audio, text, video
not_recommended_for: When discriminative prediction is the goal
children.curiosity: Ian Goodfellow proposed GANs in 2014. Diffusion models (2020-2023) surpassed GANs in quality and training stability.

children.name: GAN (Generative Adversarial Network)
children.diff_siblings: Generator and discriminator trained adversarially — different from VAE for not having explicit latent prior; from Diffusion for being single-step
not_recommended_for: State-of-the-art generation — Stable Diffusion
children.curiosity: Goodfellow published GANs in 2014 during a conversation in a bar. Yann LeCun called it 'the most interesting idea in ML in the last 10 years'.

children.name: VAE (Variational Autoencoder)
children.diff_siblings: Learns regularized latent space via Gaussian prior — stable training; different from GAN for having interpretable latent space
recommended_for: Generation with control over latent space
not_recommended_for: High-quality generation — Diffusion
children.curiosity: Kingma and Welling published VAE in 2013 developing the 'reparameterization trick' — backpropagation through stochastic samples.

children.name: Diffusion Models (DDPM/Score Matching)
children.diff_siblings: Iterative noise and denoising process — stable training; basis of Stable Diffusion and DALL-E 3; state-of-the-art quality
not_recommended_for: Real-time generation — GANs are faster
children.curiosity: Ho et al. (Google Brain) published DDPM in 2020. Stable Diffusion (2022) democratized the technology by releasing the weights openly.

children.name: Normalizing Flows
children.diff_siblings: Invertible transformations that map a simple distribution to a complex one — exactly invertible; exact log-likelihood; different from VAE and GANs
weaknesses: Restricted architecture — transformations must be invertible
not_recommended_for: Photorealistic image generation — Diffusion outperforms
children.curiosity: Rezende and Mohamed popularized Normalizing Flows in 2015. The invertibility constraint limits expressiveness compared to Diffusion.

children.name: DCGAN (Deep Convolutional GAN)
children.diff_siblings: GAN with transposed convolutions for images — different from the original GAN for using CNN architecture instead of MLP; made GANs practical for high-resolution image generation
strengths: Training much more stable than original GAN
Basis of all modern visual GANs
weaknesses: Replaced by StyleGAN for photorealistic generation
recommended_for: Educational and historical basis for GANs
not_recommended_for: State-of-the-art quality — StyleGAN or Diffusion
children.curiosity: Radford, Metz, and Chintala (OpenAI) published DCGAN in 2015. The paper established engineering practices that made GANs trainable: batch normalization, leaky ReLU, strided convolutions — and are still used today.

children.name: CycleGAN
children.diff_siblings: Image-to-image translation without training pairs — uses two GANs with a consistency cycle; different from Pix2Pix for not requiring aligned training pairs
strengths: Unpaired domain translation (horses → zebras, summer → winter)
Widely applied in artistic style and medical domain
weaknesses: Artifacts in regions with large structural differences
Replaced by Diffusion for style transfer
not_recommended_for: Maximum quality — Diffusion models outperform
children.curiosity: Zhu et al. (Berkeley) published CycleGAN in 2017. Cycle consistency (F(G(x)) ≈ x) is the central intuition — a transformed and re-transformed image must return to the original.

children.name: StyleGAN
children.diff_siblings: Style mapping-based generator — different from DCGANs for controlling high and low-level features separately via AdaIN; photorealistic generation of faces and objects
strengths: Separate style control at different scales
weaknesses: Tendency to generate artifacts in certain configurations
Replaced by Diffusion for general maximum quality
not_recommended_for: General high-quality generation — Diffusion models
children.curiosity: Karras et al. (NVIDIA) published StyleGAN in 2019. StyleGAN2 (2020) fixed 'blob artifacts' — characteristic artifacts in face images. Images on the website thispersondoesnotexist.com use StyleGAN.

children.name: WGAN (Wasserstein GAN)
children.diff_siblings: GAN with Wasserstein distance instead of Jensen-Shannon divergence — different from standard GAN for having much more stable training; critic instead of discriminator
strengths: Training much more stable than original GAN
Wasserstein distance is a meaningful metric for generation
Gradient always useful — no mode collapse due to saturation
weaknesses: Lipschitz constraints require special techniques (clipping or penalty)
Generation performance does not surpass well-trained modern GANs
recommended_for: Research and prototyping of new GAN architectures
not_recommended_for: Maximum quality — StyleGAN or Diffusion
children.curiosity: Arjovsky, Chintala, and Bottou published WGAN in 2017. The paper mathematically solved the instability problem of original GANs using optimal transport theory — connecting deep learning to 19th and 20th-century mathematics.

children.name: Flow Matching
children.diff_siblings: Generation by linear interpolation between noise and data — different from Diffusion for using straight trajectories instead of SDEs; simpler training and faster sampling
strengths: Straight trajectories — sampling in fewer steps (1-8 vs 50-1000 of Diffusion)
More efficient than DDPM in sampling speed
weaknesses: Performance still slightly inferior to Diffusion in maximum quality
recommended_for: Image generation where sampling speed is critical
not_recommended_for: Absolute maximum quality — Diffusion still dominates benchmarks
children.curiosity: Lipman et al. published Flow Matching in 2022. Stable Diffusion 3 and Meta models adopted Flow Matching as a substitute for DDPM — sampling speed is the main practical advantage.

children.name: Consistency Models
children.diff_siblings: Models that learn to map any point on the diffusion trajectory directly to the origin — allows generation in 1-2 steps without sacrificing quality; different from Diffusion for not needing multiple steps
strengths: Can be distilled from existing Diffusion models
weaknesses: Harder to train than DDPM from scratch
Very recent field — less evaluation research
recommended_for: Real-time applications where Diffusion is too slow
not_recommended_for: Maximum quality without speed constraints — Diffusion with more steps
children.curiosity: Song et al. (OpenAI) published Consistency Models in 2023. The motivation: Diffusion models work but are too slow for interactive applications. The insight: learning consistency along the diffusion trajectory eliminates the need to sample step-by-step.

children.name: 2.7 Autoencoders
children.diff_siblings: Compresses data into latent representation and reconstructs — different from PCA for being non-linear; from VAE for being deterministic; basis of feature learning and denoising
weaknesses: Representation may not be semantically meaningful
not_recommended_for: When high-quality generative models are needed — VAE/Diffusion
children.curiosity: Rumelhart, Hinton, and Williams proposed autoencoders in 1986 in the same paper as backpropagation.

children.name: Autoencoder Vanilla
children.diff_siblings: Symmetric encoder-decoder without probabilistic constraint — different from VAE for being deterministic; from Denoising AE for not adding noise
weaknesses: Can learn 'identity function' without sufficient bottleneck
not_recommended_for: When probabilistic representation is needed — VAE
children.curiosity: Hinton and Salakhutdinov demonstrated in 2006 that deep autoencoders learned better representations than PCA — reviving interest in deep networks.

children.name: Denoising Autoencoder (DAE)
children.diff_siblings: Reconstructs original input from corrupted version — different from vanilla by having richer training signal; conceptual basis of BERT (MLM is equivalent to DAE in text)
not_recommended_for: When probabilistic control is needed — VAE
children.curiosity: Vincent et al. (Montreal) proposed DAE in 2008. BERT's Masked Language Modeling is exactly DAE for text tokens.

children.name: VQ-VAE (Vector Quantized VAE)
children.diff_siblings: Discrete latent space via vector quantization — different from VAE by having discrete codes; basis of the original DALL-E
strengths: Discrete latent space — natural for tokens
not_recommended_for: Continuous latent spaces — VAE
children.curiosity: Van den Oord et al. (DeepMind) published VQ-VAE in 2017. The original DALL-E used VQ-VAE to represent images as tokens — unifying text and image in a framework.

children.name: Sparse Autoencoder
children.diff_siblings: Autoencoder with sparsity penalty on activation — different from vanilla by forcing few active activations at the same time; learns part-whole representations
strengths: Basis of the feature dictionary in LLM mechanistic interpretability
weaknesses: Choice of sparsity coefficient requires tuning
Sparse representation may lose global information
recommended_for: Extraction of localized features in images
not_recommended_for: When global representation is needed — vanilla autoencoder
children.curiosity: Olshausen and Field (1996) proposed sparse coding. Sparse Autoencoders resurged in 2023 as an interpretability tool in LLMs: Anthropic used sparse autoencoders to identify 'features' learned by Claude.

children.name: Contractive Autoencoder
children.diff_siblings: Penalizes the Frobenius norm of the encoder's Jacobian — different from Denoising AE by penalizing sensitivity to the neighborhood instead of adding noise; more robust to local variations
strengths: Connects autoencoder to data manifold geometry
weaknesses: Encoder Jacobian has high computational cost
Performance similar to Denoising AE in practice
recommended_for: Manifold learning with smooth and robust representation
not_recommended_for: When Denoising AE is already sufficient
When computational cost of Jacobian is prohibitive
children.curiosity: Rifai et al. (Montreal) published CAE in 2011. The Jacobian penalty captures the idea that small variations in data should not change the latent representation — a formalization of the concept of local robustness.

children.name: 2.8 Graph Neural Networks (GNN)
children.diff_siblings: Learns graph representations via message passing — differs from CNNs by operating on irregular topology; from RNNs by not being sequential; invariant to node permutation
not_recommended_for: Tabular data without graph structure
children.curiosity: AlphaFold2 uses GNN to model interactions between amino acids — the most impactful application of GNN in science.

children.name: GCN (Graph Convolutional Network)
children.diff_siblings: Spectral convolution via normalized Laplacian — different from GAT for having fixed weights; from GraphSAGE for being transductive
not_recommended_for: Very large graphs — GraphSAGE
Adaptive attention — GAT
children.curiosity: Kipf and Welling published GCN in 2017. The rule H' = ÃHW defines a whole family of methods.

children.name: GAT (Graph Attention Network)
children.diff_siblings: attention over neighbors — different from GCN for learning the importance of each neighbor; more flexible for heterogeneous graphs
strengths: More expressive than GCN on heterogeneous graphs
not_recommended_for: Homogeneous graphs — GCN
Very large graphs — GraphSAGE
children.curiosity: Veličković et al. published GAT in 2018. The attention mechanism was inspired by the Transformer.

children.name: GraphSAGE
children.diff_siblings: Aggregates neighborhood samples for inductive inference — different from GCN for being inductive; scales to very large graphs
strengths: Mini-batch sampling — scales to billions of nodes
not_recommended_for: Small graphs — GCN or GAT are more accurate
children.curiosity: Hamilton et al. (Stanford) published GraphSAGE in 2017. Pinterest used it for recommendation on a graph of 3 billion nodes — the first industrial application of GNN at massive scale.

children.name: GIN (Graph Isomorphism Network)
children.diff_siblings: Maximally expressive GNN — different from GCN and GAT for proving that it aggregates as expressively as the Weisfeiler-Lehman test for isomorphism; differentiates structures that GCN does not distinguish
strengths: Theoretically more expressive than GCN and GAT
Solid theoretical foundation via isomorphism theory
Differentiates graph structures that GCN cannot
weaknesses: More complex than GCN to implement
Additional expressivity rarely needed in practice
recommended_for: When differentiation of similar graph structures is critical
Molecular classification where specific subgraphs matter
not_recommended_for: When GCN or GAT are already sufficient — general cases
children.curiosity: Xu et al. (MIT and Stanford) published GIN in 2019. The theoretical result: GCN and GAT cannot distinguish certain non-isomorphic graphs — GIN was designed to be as expressive as possible within the message passing framework.

children.name: MPNN (Message Passing Neural Network)
children.diff_siblings: Unified framework for GNNs via message passing — different from GCN for being more general; unifies GCN, GAT, GraphSAGE and many other GNNs into a single formulation
strengths: Unified framework that includes GCN, GAT and GraphSAGE as special cases
Broadens the family of message passing operations
Theoretical basis for analysis and comparison of GNNs
weaknesses: High level of abstraction — hinders direct implementation
More useful as a theoretical framework than a practical model
Computational overhead compared to specific implementations
recommended_for: Research in computational chemistry and drug discovery
When a general message passing framework is needed
not_recommended_for: Practical tasks — GCN, GAT or GraphSAGE are more straightforward
children.curiosity: Gilmer et al. (Google Brain) published MPNN in 2017 for molecular property prediction. The framework unifies: each round of message passing involves 'messages' between neighbors, 'aggregation' and 'update' of each node's state.

children.name: HAN (Heterogeneous Attention Network)
children.diff_siblings: GNN for heterogeneous graphs with multiple node and edge types — different from GCN and GAT for handling graphs where nodes and edges have different types
strengths: Handles heterogeneous graphs (different node and edge types)
Attention at multiple levels: node-level and semantic-level
weaknesses: More complex than GCN for homogeneous graphs
Less scalable than GraphSAGE on very large graphs
recommended_for: Knowledge graphs with multiple entity types
not_recommended_for: Homogeneous graphs with one node type — GCN or GAT are simpler
children.curiosity: Wang et al. published HAN in 2019. Heterogeneous graphs are very common in practice: knowledge graphs have entities of different types (person, organization, place) and relations of different types (founded, works_at, located_in).

children.name: 2.9 Specialized Architectures
children.diff_siblings: Designed for specific domains — differ from general architectures by incorporating domain structural prior; less data needed for the domain; less flexibility outside it
recommended_for: When data is scarce and prior is strong
not_recommended_for: General problems without clear domain structure
children.curiosity: AlphaFold2 and PINNs exemplify specialized architectures that outperform general models even with less data.

children.name: PINN (Physics-Informed Neural Network)
children.diff_siblings: Incorporates differential equations as regularization — different from pure networks by using physical laws to guide training; mesh-free instead of discretization
strengths: Respects physical laws — more reliable extrapolation
Combines data and physics with little data
recommended_for: Physics simulation with little experimental data
not_recommended_for: When data is abundant — networks without physics work well
children.curiosity: Raissi, Perdikaris and Karniadakis published PINNs in 2019. The idea of using differential equations as regularization was revolutionary in physical simulation.

children.name: AlphaFold2
children.diff_siblings: 3D protein structure prediction — combines MSA, attention pair representation and IPA (Invariant Point Attention); solved a 50-year problem in biology
strengths: Solves 3D protein structure with atomic precision
recommended_for: Protein structure prediction and drug design
not_recommended_for: Any problem outside structural biology
children.curiosity: Jumper et al. (DeepMind) published AlphaFold2 in Nature in 2021 — considered one of the greatest scientific advances of the 21st century. Predicts structure of 200M proteins.

children.name: Neural ODE
children.diff_siblings: Uses ODE solver as network layer — continuous depth instead of discrete; constant memory at arbitrary depth
not_recommended_for: Maximum performance — ResNet and Transformer outperform
children.curiosity: Chen et al. (Toronto) published Neural ODEs in NeurIPS 2018 (Best Paper). The connection between ResNets and differential equations unified two mathematical traditions.

children.name: Matrix Factorization (Collaborative SVD)
children.diff_siblings: Matrix factorization of user-item interactions for recommendation systems — different from classical SVD for being applied to sparse matrices with implicit data; different from GNNs for being linear
strengths: Scalable to millions of users and items
weaknesses: Does not capture temporal or social context
Inferior performance to GNNs and modern DL
Cold start problem — no interaction history
recommended_for: When content features are not available
not_recommended_for: When temporal context matters — sequential systems
When content features are available — content-based filtering
children.curiosity: Koren, Bell, and Volinsky (Netflix) published the method in 2009. The BellKor team used SVD variants to win the Netflix Prize — making Matrix Factorization the standard in recommendation for a decade.

children.name: Mixture of Experts (MoE)
children.diff_siblings: Ensemble of specialized neural networks with a gating network — different from Stacking for having learned implicit specialization; basis of GPT-4 and Mixtral (models with sparse MoE)
strengths: Each expert learns to specialize in subsets of the data
Sparse MoE scales capacity without proportional cost
weaknesses: Unstable gating network — load balancing between experts is challenging
Sparse MoE implementation requires specific hardware
Less interpretable than a single model
recommended_for: Very large-scale language models (GPT-4, Mixtral, Gemini)
When parameter capacity must grow without proportional computational cost
not_recommended_for: Small datasets where specialization does not emerge
When implementation simplicity is a priority
children.curiosity: Jacobs et al. (Toronto) proposed Mixture of Experts in 1991. Shazeer et al. (Google Brain) revived the idea in 2017 with Sparsely-Gated MoE — GPT-4 and Gemini use MoE with hundreds of billions of parameters but activate only a fraction per token.

children.name: 2.10 Transfer Learning (Deep)
children.diff_siblings: Reuses pre-trained weights from large models — different from classical Transfer ML due to scale (billions of parameters); dominant paradigm in modern DL
strengths: Requires much less data for a specific task
Foundation models pre-trained on trillions of tokens
recommended_for: Any NLP, vision, or multimodal task with few data
not_recommended_for: Very specific domains without relevant pre-trained models
children.curiosity: Yosinski et al. demonstrated in 2014 that features from the first layers of CNNs are universally useful — edges and textures are the same for any visual domain.

children.name: Fine-tuning
children.diff_siblings: Adjusts all weights of the pre-trained model on the target task — different from feature extraction for updating weights; from LoRA for updating the full matrix
not_recommended_for: Very large models where LoRA is necessary
children.curiosity: Howard and Ruder proposed ULMFiT in 2018 — the first systematic fine-tuning method for NLP. BERT popularized the paradigm.

children.name: LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)
children.diff_siblings: Fine-tuning via low-rank matrices — adds only ΔW = AB; reduces trainable parameters by 10000×; basis of QLoRA for quantized models
strengths: Reduces trainable parameters from billions to millions
Original weights frozen — no catastrophic forgetting
weaknesses: Slightly lower performance than full fine-tuning
recommended_for: Fine-tuning LLMs on consumer hardware (QLoRA + LoRA)
not_recommended_for: When full fine-tuning is feasible
children.curiosity: Hu et al. (Microsoft) published LoRA in 2021. QLoRA (2023) combined 4-bit quantization with LoRA to fine-tune 65B models on a single consumer GPU.

children.name: Prompt Engineering
children.diff_siblings: Guides model via instructions without updating weights — label-free; differs from fine-tuning by not requiring labeled data; from RAG by not using an external knowledge base
strengths: Fundamental for using LLMs in production
weaknesses: Sensitive to the exact prompt format
not_recommended_for: When specific and consistent behavior is required — fine-tuning
children.curiosity: Brown et al. demonstrated few-shot prompting in GPT-3 in 2020. 'Prompt Engineering' became a discipline — chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022) improved reasoning of LLMs.

children.name: RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)
children.diff_siblings: Combines search in a knowledge base with LLM generation — differs from fine-tuning by not updating weights; differs from Prompt Engineering by using real-time external context retrieval
strengths: Reduces hallucination via grounding in real documents
weaknesses: Quality dependent on the retrieval system
Additional latency due to the retrieval step
Engineering complexity for indexing and updating
recommended_for: When the LLM's knowledge is outdated or insufficient
not_recommended_for: When fine-tuning already captures all necessary knowledge
When latency is critical — RAG adds overhead
children.curiosity: Lewis et al. (Facebook AI) published RAG in 2020. The RAG paradigm became standard in enterprise AI systems in 2023 — allows LLMs to access updated knowledge bases without retraining.

children.name: 3. Classical Statistics
children.diff_siblings: Derives models from mathematical and probabilistic principles — differs from ML by prioritizing inference, interpretability, and theoretical guarantees; from DL by having explicit assumptions about distributions
strengths: Rigorous statistical inference with p-values and intervals
Theoretical guarantees of consistency and efficiency
weaknesses: Inferior predictive performance compared to ML/DL on complex data
recommended_for: Science, medicine, and social sciences where inference is the goal
Small to medium data where ML overfits
not_recommended_for: Pure prediction with abundant data — ML outperforms
Image and text data — DL outperforms
children.curiosity: The Bayesian vs. Frequentist debate lasted over a century. Modern computing (MCMC) solved the practical problem, but the philosophy remains controversial.

children.name: 3.1 Structural Equations (SEM)
children.diff_siblings: Models direct and indirect relationships between latent and observed variables — differs from regression by modeling latent variables; from Bayesian networks by having parameters estimated by MLE
strengths: Decomposes effects into direct and indirect
not_recommended_for: All variables observed — multiple regression is sufficient
When causal structure is unknown
children.curiosity: Wright developed path analysis in 1920 for genetic inheritance. Jöreskog generalized to SEM with latent variables in the 1970s.

children.name: SEM (Structural Equation Modeling)
children.diff_siblings: System of equations with latent variables — differs from regression by modeling latent structure; from CFA by including structural relationships between constructs
strengths: Decomposes direct, indirect, and total effects
weaknesses: Identification requires at least 3 indicators per factor
not_recommended_for: Data with n < 100 — unstable estimation
Directly measurable variables — regression
children.curiosity: Jöreskog developed LISREL in 1969 combining confirmatory factor analysis with simultaneous regression.

children.name: CFA (Confirmatory Factor Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: Tests pre-specified factor structure — differs from EFA by having a priori hypothesized structure; confirms or refutes measurement model
strengths: Formal test of theoretical factor structure
weaknesses: Fit indices misleading with large n
not_recommended_for: When structure is unknown — EFA
children.curiosity: Jöreskog formalized CFA in 1969. The EFA/CFA distinction is central in psychometrics: EFA explores, CFA confirms.

children.name: EFA (Exploratory Factor Analysis)
children.diff_siblings: Extracts latent factors without pre-specified structure — differs from CFA by being exploratory; from PCA by modeling common variance (not total)
weaknesses: Solution not unique — rotation is arbitrary
not_recommended_for: When factor structure is known — CFA
children.curiosity: Spearman proposed EFA in 1904 seeking the 'g' factor of intelligence. The debate on the correct number of factors continues — eigenvalue > 1, scree plot and parallel analysis frequently disagree.

children.name: 3.2 Count and Proportion Models
children.diff_siblings: For non-negative integer responses or proportions — differ from linear regression by respecting the natural domain; from simple GLMs by treating overdispersion or zero inflation explicitly
strengths: Extensions for overdispersion and excessive zeros
recommended_for: When overdispersion or excessive zeros are present
not_recommended_for: When Poisson is already adequate
Continuous data where linear regression is sufficient
children.curiosity: Overdispersion — variance greater than the mean — is the rule, not the exception, in real data. Negative Binomial and Zero-Inflated models exist because Poisson is an idealization rarely satisfied.

children.name: Negative Binomial
children.diff_siblings: Extension of Poisson for overdispersion — dispersion parameter θ; different from Poisson by having variance > mean; from ZIP by not having zero inflation
not_recommended_for: Data with many zeros — Zero-Inflated
children.curiosity: Negative Binomial was proposed in 1920 to model variation in accident susceptibility. COVID-19 showed extreme overdispersion — few people cause many transmissions.

children.name: Zero-Inflated Poisson (ZIP)
children.diff_siblings: Mixture of zero excess process and Poisson — different from Poisson by modeling structural zeros separately; from Negative Binomial by not modeling overdispersion
strengths: Interpretation of the two components is clear
weaknesses: More parameters than Poisson or NB
recommended_for: Health data with many non-users of services
not_recommended_for: Overdispersion without excessive zeros — NB
children.curiosity: Lambert proposed ZIP in 1992 for defects in manufacturing — many parts have zero defects because they are perfect (structural zero).

children.name: Hurdle Model
children.diff_siblings: Two-part model — binary to cross the zero 'hurdle', and truncated for positive counts; different from ZIP because it has no random zeros (only structural zeros)
strengths: Explicit modeling of the non-zero process
recommended_for: Health: probability of using service and quantity given use
not_recommended_for: When random zeros exist — ZIP
children.curiosity: Mullahy proposed Hurdle Models in 1986 for health economics. ZIP assumes zeros from two processes; Hurdle assumes zeros and positives are completely separate processes.

children.name: Zero-and-One Inflated Beta Regression
children.diff_siblings: Extension of Beta Regression for data with exact zeros and ones — different from Beta Regression by adding probability mass at 0 and/or 1
strengths: Covers practical cases of proportions with extremes
not_recommended_for: Data without zeros and ones — Beta Regression
Binary data — Logistic
children.curiosity: Ospina and Ferrari developed Zero-and-One Inflated Beta Regression in 2010. For engagement data — where users can have 0% or 100% click-through rate — inflation at 0 and 1 is necessary.

children.name: ANOVA / ANCOVA
children.diff_siblings: Analysis of Variance and Covariance — tests differences between groups; differs from linear regression by focusing on variance decomposition; from GLMs by being the historical formulation of hypothesis testing with categorical predictors
strengths: Tests multiple groups simultaneously without type I error inflation
weaknesses: The same as regression with dummies — historical formulation
recommended_for: Scientific research with analysis of variance as standard
not_recommended_for: Non-normal data — transformation or non-parametric models
Models with more than 2-3 predictors — multiple regression
children.curiosity: Ronald Fisher developed ANOVA in 1918 studying agricultural data at Rothamsted Research. ANOVA was the dominant tool in experimental research for 70 years — before being recognized as a special case of linear regression with dummy variables.

children.name: 3.3 Bayesian Models
children.diff_siblings: Incorporate prior in estimation and return posterior distribution — differ from frequentist by modeling parametric uncertainty explicitly; computationally intensive
recommended_for: Sparse data where prior is informative
When full parameter distribution is necessary
not_recommended_for: Big data where frequentists are equivalent and faster
children.curiosity: Harold Jeffreys (Bayesian) and Ronald Fisher (Frequentist) were contemporaries and intellectual rivals. Modern computing (MCMC) solved the practical problem.

children.name: MCMC (Markov Chain Monte Carlo)
children.diff_siblings: Sampling the posterior via Markov chain — different from VI by being asymptotically exact; tools: Stan, PyMC
weaknesses: Slow for models with many parameters
recommended_for: Scientific models with exact posterior necessary
not_recommended_for: Big data — VI is much faster
children.curiosity: The Metropolis algorithm (1953) was developed by physicists from the Manhattan Project to simulate molecules. Stan (2012) democratized MCMC with efficient HMC.

children.name: Variational Inference (VI)
children.diff_siblings: Approximates posterior via parametric family optimizing ELBO — different from MCMC for being faster; less accurate; basis of VAEs and LLMs with uncertainty
strengths: Gradients allow integration with deep learning
weaknesses: Approximate posterior can be very different from the true one
not_recommended_for: When posterior is highly non-Gaussian — MCMC
children.curiosity: Blei, Kucukelbir, and McAuliffe published a review of VI in 2017. The connection with deep learning via VAE made VI central in modern ML.

children.name: Gaussian Process (GP) as prior
children.diff_siblings: Prior over functions via kernel — different from GP Regression by the angle; basis of Bayesian optimization and field modeling
strengths: Bayesian optimization uses GP for efficient exploration
not_recommended_for: Big data — Deep GP or sparse GP are necessary
children.curiosity: Gaussian Processes were popularized by Rasmussen and Williams in 2006. Every hyperparameter tuning with Optuna or similar uses a GP internally.

children.name: Hierarchical Bayesian Models
children.diff_siblings: Hierarchical prior where hyperparameters have their own prior — different from flat MCMC for having automatic shrinkage; from LMM for having full Bayesian inference
strengths: Estimates both specific effects and pool
Full uncertainty in parameters of all levels
recommended_for: When individual group estimates are very uncertain
not_recommended_for: Data with many observations per group — LMM is equivalent and faster
children.curiosity: Lindley and Smith (1972) formalized hierarchical Bayesian models. Andrew Gelman popularized them via 'Bayesian Data Analysis' (1995).

children.name: Copula Models (Bayesian)
children.diff_siblings: Models dependency between variables via copula — different from Pearson correlation for capturing non-linear dependencies and tail risk; from Bayesian Networks for not having DAG structure
strengths: Marginals and dependency are modeled separately
weaknesses: Choice of copula family is critical
recommended_for: Joint financial risk — portfolios in extreme scenarios
not_recommended_for: Data with simple linear dependency — Pearson correlation
children.curiosity: Sklar proved in 1959 that any multivariate distribution can be decomposed into marginals and a copula. David Li's Gaussian Copula contributed to the 2008 financial crisis.

children.name: INLA (Integrated Nested Laplace Approximation)
children.diff_siblings: Bayesian inference via nested Laplace approximation — different from MCMC for being analytical and much faster; especially efficient for GLMMs and Gaussian latent field models
strengths: 100-1000× faster than MCMC for supported models
Exact for Gaussian latent field models
R-INLA is a reference in spatial epidemiology
weaknesses: Limited to Gaussian latent field models
R-INLA interface has a learning curve
recommended_for: Spatial epidemiology with complex random effects
Any Bayesian GLMM where MCMC is slow
not_recommended_for: Models outside the Gaussian latent field family — MCMC
children.curiosity: Rue, Martino, and Chopin published INLA in 2009. R-INLA made Bayesian inference practical for epidemiologists — before, a hierarchical model that took days via MCMC could be fitted in seconds with INLA.

children.name: Empirical Bayes
children.diff_siblings: Estimates the prior from data before using it for inference — different from full Bayes because it uses data to specify the prior; from frequentist methods because it still uses a Bayesian framework
strengths: Computes middle ground between full Bayes and frequentist
weaknesses: Using data to specify the prior and then for inference violates Bayesian principles
Less principled than full hierarchical Bayes
recommended_for: Large collections of similar problems where information pooling helps
not_recommended_for: When the prior can be specified without the data
When full uncertainty in the prior parameters is necessary — hierarchical Bayes
children.curiosity: Herbert Robbins proposed Empirical Bayes in 1956. The James-Stein estimator (1961) — which 'shrinks' estimates toward the overall mean — is a special case of Empirical Bayes and was one of the first examples of an inadmissible estimator outperformed by another.

children.name: 3.4 Expert Systems and Rule-Based Models
children.diff_siblings: Encode domain knowledge in explicit rules — differ from ML because they do not learn from data; from formal logic because they handle uncertainty; historically important as the first AI approach
weaknesses: Explicitly coded knowledge is costly to maintain
recommended_for: Domains with well-defined and stable rules
When traceability is a legal requirement
not_recommended_for: Domains with frequent exceptions
When learning from data is feasible
children.curiosity: MYCIN (1972) was the first successful medical expert system. But it required constant maintenance of 600 rules — any change in protocol required manual update.

children.name: Fuzzy Logic Systems
children.diff_siblings: Logic with degrees of truth in [0,1] instead of binary {0,1} — models linguistic imprecision; different from probability because it represents imprecision, not random uncertainty
weaknesses: Definition of membership functions is subjective
Inferior performance to ML in classification tasks
recommended_for: Control of embedded systems (autofocus camera, washing machine)
not_recommended_for: Classification and regression — ML outperforms
children.curiosity: Lotfi Zadeh proposed Fuzzy Logic in 1965. Matsushita (Panasonic) launched the first fuzzy washing machine in 1990 in Japan — a commercial success. Gradually replaced by ML in learning applications.

children.name: Expert System with Rules (RETE)
children.diff_siblings: Rete algorithm for efficient evaluation of rules in production systems — different from fuzzy logic because it is binary; from ML because it has explicit rules created by experts
strengths: Efficient RETE algorithm for many rules
weaknesses: Rules must be written and maintained manually
recommended_for: Medical diagnostic systems with fixed protocols
not_recommended_for: Domains with many exceptions — ML is more adaptable
children.curiosity: Charles Forgy developed RETE in 1979. CLIPS (NASA, 1985) is still used in mission-critical embedded systems where deterministic behavior is necessary.

children.name: Decision Trees as Business Rules
children.diff_siblings: Explicit use of trees to create and communicate business rules — different from predictive CART because it is a knowledge management tool; rules validated and audited by experts
strengths: Combine data learning with expert validation
weaknesses: Depth must be limited for maintainability
not_recommended_for: Maximum performance — ensemble outperforms
children.curiosity: The use of trees for business rules predates ML — decision flowcharts existed in the 1950s. The difference: the tree is learned from data but then validated and edited by experts.
